lessons.title: Meet Chat and Code
lessons.summary: Know which side to use before you start.
lessons.location: Open the navigation menu, then choose Chat or Code.
before: You can read this guide without an account or an internet connection.

steps.title: Use Chat for a conversation
steps.body: Ask questions, write, study, research, discuss images, or request a small interactive visual. Chat can use its allowed research, memory, history, GitHub-reading, and app-settings tools.

steps.title: Use Code for project work
steps.body: Choose Code when you want the assistant to edit project files, run commands, build something, or use connected development tools. Choose a workspace so it knows which files belong to the task.

steps.title: Find the supporting screens
steps.body: Use the navigation menu for projects, conversations, files, terminal, automation, and Settings. On wide layouts, some of these appear beside the conversation.

steps.title: Follow a lesson, then try it
steps.body: Every lesson has a Where to go box and buttons that open the relevant app screen. Save a lesson with its bookmark, or mark it as learned. The back arrow returns through the guide.

lessons.outcome: You can choose Chat for an explanation and Code for a change to a real project.
limits: Chat cannot silently edit your workspace or run shell commands. A request for project work may offer a handoff to Code.
The model you choose affects quality, tool use, vision, cost, and speed. Installing AndroidHarness does not grant access to every AI model.

fixes.solution: Open Settings and search for the control or its English name. Coding-specific settings also live under Coding.

lessons.title: Send your first message
lessons.summary: Get a working conversation without setting up a coding environment.
lessons.location: Navigation menu → Chat → model name in the header.
before: Connect to the internet for a hosted model, or install a supported local model first.

steps.title: Choose a model
steps.body: Tap the model name. Choose Harness if a built-in free model is available, a provider you connected, a signed-in ChatGPT account, or an installed local model.

steps.title: Start with a small request
steps.body: Type one clear question and send it. For example, ask for an explanation with a short example. A small first message makes connection problems easier to identify.

steps.title: Read the response and its activity
steps.body: The reply appears as it arrives. Thinking and tool activity can be expanded when present. Search citations are useful links to check, not a guarantee that the answer is correct.

steps.title: Keep talking
steps.body: Ask a follow-up in the same conversation. Open a new Chat when you want a separate topic. Your conversations stay in the app until you remove them.

lessons.outcome: A reply appears in your conversation, and you can ask a follow-up.
limits: Harness free-model availability and limits are controlled by its upstream services; free access is not guaranteed.
Regular Chat does not require Linux, GitHub, root, or wireless debugging. Hosted replies still require a working connection and provider access.

fixes.solution: Check the selected provider and model. If a free service is busy or limited, wait or choose another connection. See the API error lesson for key and billing errors.

lessons.example: Explain how an Android app works as if I am new to programming. Give me one small example.

lessons.title: Finish a small coding task
lessons.summary: Try the full loop: inspect, change, and check.
lessons.location: Navigation menu → Code → workspace selector.
before: Choose a model that can use tools.
Start with a small project you are comfortable changing.

steps.title: Choose a workspace
steps.body: Select an existing project or create one from the workspace picker. A workspace is the folder that Code will inspect and change; check its name before sending a request.

steps.title: Describe the outcome
steps.body: Say what should change and how you will know it works. You can start in Plan to inspect the project before switching to Act for edits.

steps.title: Review requests for permission
steps.body: If an approval appears, read the command, affected files, or preview. Approve the action you intend, or decline it and explain how to proceed.

steps.title: Check the result
steps.body: Read the final response, inspect the file changes, and run the project checks. An assistant saying it is finished is different from a passing test or a working preview.

lessons.outcome: Your project has a reviewable change, with any test results or remaining limitations shown in the conversation.
limits: A tool-capable model and accessible workspace are required for reliable project work.
Commands may need the optional Linux environment or packages. The app cannot promise that every desktop project runs unchanged on Android.

fixes.problem: The assistant only explains a change
fixes.solution: Confirm that you opened Code, chose the correct workspace, and selected Act when you want the change applied.

lessons.title: API keys, credits, and subscriptions
lessons.summary: Understand what you are paying for before connecting a service.
lessons.location: A provider’s official developer console, then Settings → Models & providers → Manage providers.
before: Choose the provider whose models you want to use. An API key belongs to that provider.

steps.title: Understand the key
steps.body: An API key is a secret credential. It lets AndroidHarness send requests to your provider account. Creating a key does not itself buy a model, fund an account, or make requests unlimited.

steps.title: Check the billing route
steps.body: Open the provider’s developer billing page. It may offer a free allowance, prepaid credits, usage-based billing, or a plan. Read the model price and usage limits shown for your account.

steps.title: Activate access if needed
steps.body: Use the provider’s own checkout to add a payment method, buy credits, or activate a suitable plan. Check automatic top-ups and spending controls before confirming. AndroidHarness does not sell provider API subscriptions.

steps.title: Keep an eye on usage
steps.body: After a short test in the app, check the provider’s usage dashboard. Long conversations, research, retries, thinking, and multiple agents can all increase usage.

lessons.outcome: Your developer account has the access you intended, and you know where to view its balance, limits, and charges.
limits: A consumer chat subscription and API billing are different access paths. Some subscriptions offer API credits that must be claimed; check the provider’s current benefits.
App cost estimates and task budgets are useful guides. They are not a guaranteed billing cap at the provider.

fixes.problem: I paid for a chat app but my API key fails
fixes.solution: Check the developer console for API access, available credits, and any subscription-credit linking step. Alternatively use a supported sign-in connection in AndroidHarness.

lessons.keywords: buy purchase subscription payment billing API tokens credits pricing

lessons.title: Add and use an API key
lessons.summary: Connect a model provider in a few deliberate steps.
lessons.location: Settings → Models & providers → Manage providers → Add provider. You can also manage providers from the model picker.
before: Have a valid key from the provider’s official console.
Use a key for the same service as the provider you select.

steps.title: Choose the provider
steps.body: Tap Add provider and pick its name. The app fills in the usual protocol and address for curated providers; choose Custom endpoint only when you need to supply these yourself.

steps.title: Enter the key
steps.body: Paste the secret into the API key field. Give the connection a useful name if you have more than one. Do not paste the key into an ordinary chat message.

steps.title: Choose a model and save
steps.body: Continue to the model step. Choose a model offered by your account, then save the connection. If a catalogue request fails, read the error before entering a model ID manually.

steps.title: Select it for the conversation
steps.body: Return to Chat or Code, tap the header’s model name, and choose this provider and model. Send a small test message before starting a long task.

lessons.outcome: The provider is saved and the conversation header shows your chosen model.
limits: Saving a connection does not guarantee access to every model in a cached catalogue. The provider checks your key, balance, permissions, and model access when used.
Keys are saved in the app’s encrypted credential storage. Revoking a key at the provider is the way to invalidate it outside the app.

fixes.problem: The connection is saved but another model answers
fixes.solution: Reopen the model picker for this conversation. Its selection can differ from the app default or the planning/execution selections.

lessons.title: Connect an OpenAI API key
lessons.summary: Set up API access and choose the OpenAI connection type.
lessons.location: OpenAI developer platform → API keys and Billing; AndroidHarness → Manage providers.
before: Use the OpenAI account and API organization you intend to pay with.

steps.title: Prepare the API account
steps.body: Open the official developer quickstart below and sign in to the API platform. Choose the intended organization/project and check its billing access and available credits.

steps.title: Create a key
steps.body: Create a project API key, give it a recognizable name, and copy the secret while it is displayed. Keep it private.

steps.title: Add it to AndroidHarness
steps.body: In Manage providers, choose OpenAI or OpenAI (Responses). Paste the key, continue, select an available model, and save.

steps.title: Confirm the connection
steps.body: Select the saved model in a conversation and send a short request. Check the API dashboard if the provider reports billing, permissions, or quota problems.

lessons.outcome: Your conversation can use the selected OpenAI API model.
limits: The two OpenAI presets use different API protocols. Model support can differ; use the protocol supported by the selected model.
Signing in through Connected accounts is a separate route. Eligible subscription API-credit benefits may need activation in the API organization.

fixes.problem: I cannot see a key I created earlier
fixes.solution: Create a replacement in the official platform, update this connection, and revoke the old key if appropriate.

lessons.title: Connect Claude through the API
lessons.summary: Create an Anthropic key and check its API funding.
lessons.location: Claude Console → API keys and Billing; AndroidHarness → Manage providers → Anthropic.
before: Have access to the intended Claude API organization or workspace.

steps.title: Open the official Console
steps.body: Use the official API-key guide below to reach the current Claude Console. Sign in or create an account.

steps.title: Create an API key
steps.body: Open API keys, create a named key, choose its owner/scope and expiry where offered, and copy the secret when it is shown.

steps.title: Check API billing
steps.body: Open the Console billing page. Activate the access or credits required by your account. Do not assume that a consumer Claude subscription automatically funds this API key.

steps.title: Save and test
steps.body: Choose Anthropic in AndroidHarness, paste the key, select a model available to your account, and save. Select it in Chat or Code and send a short request.

lessons.outcome: A saved Anthropic connection can answer with the model you selected.
limits: Model availability, thinking options, spending limits, and regional access are decided by the provider.
An API key with insufficient permissions or balance will still fail even if its format looks correct.

fixes.solution: Check the billing page for the organization that owns this key. Adding a key to AndroidHarness does not add funds.

lessons.title: Connect a Gemini API key
lessons.summary: Use Google AI Studio and choose the right project.
lessons.location: Google AI Studio → API keys; AndroidHarness → Manage providers → Gemini.
before: Use a Google account and project eligible for the Gemini API.

steps.title: Create or choose a project
steps.body: Open Google AI Studio’s API keys page. Use the project you want to associate with this connection, then create or copy its API key.

steps.title: Choose a billing tier deliberately
steps.body: Eligible models may have a free allowance. To enable paid access, use Set up billing for that project and follow the account’s current prepay or billing steps.

steps.title: Add the Gemini connection
steps.body: Choose Gemini in AndroidHarness, paste the key, continue to the model list, and save a model offered to your account.

steps.title: Try a short message
steps.body: Choose the model in Chat or Code. If it fails, check that the key’s project, enabled API, billing status, and model limits match your request.

lessons.outcome: AndroidHarness can reach Gemini using the key attached to the project you chose.
limits: Free and paid tiers have different limits and terms. Check the current official billing page before using sensitive data or making purchases.
A model supporting images does not make every provider feature available through this app. Only implemented conversation and tool capabilities are exposed.

fixes.problem: Billing is enabled but I still hit a limit
fixes.solution: Check the exact project and model quota in AI Studio. A rate limit and an empty credit balance require different fixes.

lessons.title: Connect OpenRouter
lessons.summary: Use one connection to choose from OpenRouter’s model catalogue.
lessons.location: OpenRouter → Settings → Keys and Credits; AndroidHarness → Manage providers → OpenRouter.
before: Have an OpenRouter account. Check each chosen model’s price and access requirements.

steps.title: Create a key
steps.body: Open the official OpenRouter site, sign in, and create an API key in Keys. Use any key-level credit limit or expiry you need.

steps.title: Check your credits
steps.body: Use the official Credits/Billing area to fund paid requests. Review fees, top-ups, and free-model limits shown for your account before buying.

steps.title: Connect in the app
steps.body: Choose OpenRouter, paste the key, and select a model from its catalogue. Keep the complete model ID, including its provider prefix or variant suffix.

steps.title: Check the selected model
steps.body: Select it in Chat or Code and test a small request. Pick a tool-capable model for Code and an image-capable model for image questions.

lessons.outcome: The conversation uses the OpenRouter model you selected.
limits: OpenRouter models can have different upstream providers, prices, privacy policies, and capabilities.
A free-labelled model can still have availability and rate restrictions. A saved key does not remove them.

fixes.solution: Refresh the model list and choose an available entry. Do not shorten the ID to just the display name.

lessons.title: Groq, DeepSeek, Mistral, Together, and more
lessons.summary: Use a curated provider or search the wider provider directory.
lessons.location: Manage providers → Add provider → choose or search a provider.
before: Have an API account with the service you choose.

steps.title: Choose the matching service
steps.body: Curated choices include Groq, DeepSeek, Together, Mistral, and A2Agent. The wider directory may show additional services. Choose the service that issued your key.

steps.title: Get a key from its official console
steps.body: Sign in on that service’s own website and open its API keys area. Create a key for your intended account/workspace. Use the official setup links below for the listed services.

steps.title: Enable the access you need
steps.body: Check Billing, Credits, or Plans in that console. Some accounts offer a limited free tier; paid models may need credits or a payment method. Follow the terms shown there.

steps.title: Save and select a model
steps.body: Paste the key into the matching AndroidHarness connection, choose an offered model, and save. Select that model in the conversation header and test it.

lessons.outcome: The chosen service is available in your model picker.
limits: The directory describes potential connections; it does not guarantee that your account can use every advertised model.
Groq speech settings use a separate Voice & speech key field. Adding Groq as a chat provider does not automatically configure that field.

fixes.solution: Refresh/search the provider directory. If it is compatible with a supported protocol, use Custom endpoint with its official base URL and model ID.

lessons.title: Custom endpoints, Ollama, and LM Studio
lessons.summary: Connect a compatible API server, including one on another computer.
lessons.location: Manage providers → Add provider → Ollama, LM Studio, or Custom endpoint.
before: Have a running server that implements a supported protocol.
For a remote computer, know its reachable address and any authentication it requires.

steps.title: Choose a protocol
steps.body: For a custom connection, match the server’s documented protocol: OpenAI-compatible chat, OpenAI Responses, Anthropic, or Gemini. These formats are not interchangeable.

steps.title: Enter the server address
steps.body: Use the API base URL, not a website’s chat page. The Ollama and LM Studio presets start with a loopback address. On your phone, 127.0.0.1 means your phone.

steps.title: Add credentials and a model
steps.body: For a server on your computer, replace the address with its reachable LAN address or another connection you control. Set any required key/headers and use an actual installed model ID.

steps.title: Test from the phone
steps.body: Make sure the server is listening on a reachable interface and the network allows the connection. Save the provider and send a small request from AndroidHarness.

lessons.outcome: The phone can talk to the compatible server and receive a model reply.
limits: A desktop model server is different from the app’s on-device Local models feature.
AndroidHarness does not start Ollama or LM Studio on your computer or automatically create a network tunnel.

fixes.solution: Check the server process, listening address, port, phone network, and firewall. A desktop localhost address is not reachable as phone localhost.

lessons.keywords: localhost LAN remote Ollama LM Studio modules

lessons.title: Manage keys, headers, and proxies
lessons.summary: Edit a connection without losing its other credentials.
lessons.location: Manage providers → connection options → Connection controls, or edit the provider.
before: Know which saved provider connection you want to change.

steps.title: Review the key list
steps.body: Add separate named keys, enable or disable them, and use the eye control only when you need to see a value. Keep at least the credentials required by that service enabled.

steps.title: Rotate a key safely
steps.body: Add the replacement key and test the connection before removing an old key. Remove or revoke a compromised key at the provider as well as in the app.

steps.title: Configure advanced networking only if needed
steps.body: Connection controls include proxy settings and custom request headers. Use the server’s documented header names and values; keep secrets in credential fields.

steps.title: Review providers and models
steps.body: Use provider management to refresh catalogues, hide or show models, add a custom model ID, and organize the choices you use. Reopen the conversation picker to select the result.

lessons.outcome: The connection has the intended active keys and networking options, and your model list is easier to browse.
limits: Key rotation can retry a rejected credential; it cannot guarantee extra quota or bypass a provider’s limits.
Proxy addresses and custom headers affect where requests go. Only use networking settings you understand and trust.

fixes.problem: Everything fails after a networking change
fixes.solution: Check the proxy host/port, credentials, custom headers, and API base URL. Restore the last working configuration and test one small request.

lessons.title: Choose models and thinking levels
lessons.summary: Make the choice for the conversation you are actually using.
lessons.location: Chat or Code → model name and thinking control in the header.
before: Have a connected provider, signed-in account, or installed local model.

steps.title: Pick a provider and model
steps.body: Open the model picker, search or browse providers, then choose a model. Hidden models can be managed from provider settings. Refresh the catalogue when available if a model has changed.

steps.title: Choose the selection scope
steps.body: Pay attention to whether you are changing the app default or this conversation. With separate planning/execution enabled, choose the model for the relevant role.

steps.title: Set thinking when supported
steps.body: Open the thinking control and choose an offered effort, toggle, or budget. Available controls depend on the model and API. Custom reasoning choices do not add capabilities a model lacks.

steps.title: Match capabilities to your task
steps.body: Use tool support for Code and image input for attachments that need vision. If a model rejects a capability, choose another model or remove that input.

lessons.outcome: The header shows your chosen model and thinking choice for the current task.
limits: More thinking can increase time and token use. It does not guarantee a correct answer.
Provider metadata may be incomplete. A model appearing in a list is not proof of tool or image support.

fixes.problem: The setting changes another conversation too
fixes.solution: Check the picker’s selection scope and app defaults. Existing conversations can retain their own model choice.

lessons.title: Planning models and fallback
lessons.summary: Choose separate roles and decide what happens when a provider fails.
lessons.location: Settings → Models & providers.
before: Connect the providers you intend to use before building a fallback list.

steps.title: Set the normal selection
steps.body: Check the current setup shown on the page. This is the starting point for selections that use the app default.

steps.title: Separate Plan and Act if useful
steps.body: Enable the planning/execution model option and choose a provider/model for each role. Plan is for inspection and a proposed approach; Act can carry out permitted actions.

steps.title: Review fallback policy
steps.body: Open the fallback controls and choose when switching is allowed, which models may be tried, and any available retry settings. Read the privacy/routing notice before enabling another service.

steps.title: Try a short task
steps.body: Check the conversation header and run activity so you know which provider/model is actually serving the task. Change or disable a fallback you do not want.

lessons.outcome: Your model roles and permitted fallbacks reflect how you want work routed.
limits: Fallback can send conversation context to a different configured provider and may incur that provider’s charges.
A fallback model must support the inputs and tools needed by the request. Not every failed request can be recovered automatically.

fixes.solution: Refresh the connection, check its key and model access, and remove stale entries. Retrying a billing failure without changing access will not fix it.

lessons.title: Sign in with ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Use the app’s connected-account route when your account is eligible.
lessons.location: Settings → Connected accounts.
before: Have a ChatGPT account and a browser that can finish sign-in.

steps.title: Start sign-in
steps.body: Choose Add account or the sign-in action. Finish the official browser authorization and return to AndroidHarness. You can cancel a pending sign-in from the account panel.

steps.title: Choose the connected account
steps.body: Select the account you want to use. The app shows the models offered to that account rather than assuming every model is available.

steps.title: Pick a model for the conversation
steps.body: Open the model picker and select the connected account and one of its models. Check the header before sending.

steps.title: Manage access
steps.body: Use Refresh, Check models, Reconnect, and usage controls when needed. Sign out an account you no longer want stored on the phone.

lessons.outcome: The connected account appears as a selectable model connection.
limits: Eligibility, models, rate limits, and plan usage are controlled by OpenAI. A successful browser login is not a promise of unlimited model access.
This sign-in route is separate from adding an OpenAI API key and its developer billing.

fixes.problem: The account shows no models or asks to reconnect
fixes.solution: Use the panel’s reconnect/refresh controls. Check the selected account’s access in the official service before choosing an available model.

lessons.title: Use the optional 9Router connection
lessons.summary: Install and run the local routing service when you need it.
lessons.location: Settings → 9Router.
before: A working Linux environment and enough storage/network access for installation.
Any external accounts required by the routing service.

steps.title: Install from the 9Router page
steps.body: Read the page’s description and run its install action. Wait for the installation status before continuing.

steps.title: Start the local service
steps.body: Use Start and wait for the service to report running. The dashboard is a local page on this device.

steps.title: Configure its dashboard
steps.body: Open the dashboard and connect only services you are entitled to use. Follow the router’s own instructions for its supported accounts and model routes.

steps.title: Use and stop it
steps.body: Use the app’s connection action when available, then choose its model in the picker. Return here to stop the service or review logs if you no longer need it.

lessons.outcome: The router is running locally and a compatible route can be chosen as a provider.
limits: A router does not grant paid access, create credits, or guarantee that an external service supports your intended use.
Its service must remain available while requests use it. This is optional; ordinary provider connections do not need it.

fixes.problem: The dashboard or model request fails
fixes.solution: Check the local service state and logs, then the router’s account/route configuration. Restart only after reading the reported failure.

lessons.title: Ask about files and images
lessons.summary: Attach something useful and make sure it is ready before sending.
lessons.location: Chat or Code → attachment control beside the message box.
before: For image questions, choose a model with image input.
Use a document you are allowed to share with the selected provider.

steps.title: Attach the file
steps.body: Use the attachment picker and choose the image or supported document. Wait for its preparation state before sending; remove the attachment if you chose the wrong item.

steps.title: Tell the assistant what to look for
steps.body: Ask a specific question, such as comparing two screenshots or summarizing the text you attached. Name the attachment if you include more than one.

steps.title: Check what was readable
steps.body: Text and readable PDFs can be extracted for the model. A scanned PDF may have no extractable text. For a visual detail, attach a clear image to a vision-capable model.

steps.title: Inspect image replies
steps.body: Tap an image to open the viewer and zoom it. In Chat, the assistant also has image-inspection/zoom tools when the model supports them.

lessons.outcome: The attachment is included with your message, and the response refers to its actual contents.
limits: File size, text extraction, context budgets, and model capabilities can limit how much can be read.
Attaching a file to Chat does not make Chat a workspace editor. For changes to real project files, use Code.

fixes.problem: The assistant cannot read a PDF
fixes.solution: Check that text can be selected in the PDF. Supply a text version or clear screenshots when extraction is unavailable.

lessons.title: Research with web search and page reading
lessons.summary: Choose how much research you want, then check the sources.
lessons.location: Chat → research-depth control; Settings → Web search for the search connection.
before: A working internet connection.
A model that can call the available research tools.

steps.title: Choose a depth
steps.body: The header offers Off, Instant, Deep, Auto, Deep research, and Max research. Use a lighter option for a quick question and a deeper option when you want more investigation.

steps.title: Set up search if needed
steps.body: Keyless search needs no search API key. For Brave or Tavily, select that backend in Settings → Web search, obtain its own key, and use the app’s verification/save action.

steps.title: Give the question boundaries
steps.body: Specify the subject, date range, place, and what evidence matters. Paste a direct link if you want a particular page read. Ask for dates and sources for time-sensitive claims.

steps.title: Follow the evidence
steps.body: Open source links and inspect the Sources in this chat library. Ask a follow-up about gaps, conflicting claims, or a page that could not be read.

lessons.outcome: The answer includes relevant sources when research succeeds, and you can open the pages yourself.
limits: Search keys are separate from model-provider keys. A model key does not automatically enable Brave or Tavily.
Paywalls, logins, blocked websites, unavailable Reddit pages, and network failures can prevent reading. Deeper research uses more time and model/tool requests.

fixes.solution: Try another query or a direct URL. Check the selected search backend and key; keyless search can also be limited by public search engines.

lessons.title: Charts, diagrams, widgets, and mockups
lessons.summary: Ask for a visual explanation or a small interactive idea.
lessons.location: Chat → send a request for a chart, diagram, calculator, illustration, or interface mockup.
before: Choose a model that follows visual-response instructions well.
Provide the real data when the visual must represent facts.

steps.title: Describe the visual goal
steps.body: Say what you want to understand or compare. For a mockup, describe the audience, screen, content, and intended interactions.

steps.title: Ask for an inline visual
steps.body: Chat can render supported rich components and self-contained HTML/SVG responses inside the conversation. For example, ask for a slider that illustrates how a value changes.

steps.title: Explore it
steps.body: Use the controls in an interactive response and check the labels/data. If the result is unclear, request one specific adjustment in a follow-up.

steps.title: Move to Code for a real implementation
steps.body: A conversational mockup is a useful sketch. Use the Code handoff when you want project files, dependencies, a working site/app, or a saved artifact built and tested.

lessons.outcome: A supported visual appears inside the reply; interactive controls work within that preview when the model produced valid content.
limits: Inline HTML/SVG runs in a restricted preview without a native app bridge or network access. It cannot control your phone or act as a full installed app.
A drawn illustration is different from a dedicated image-generation service. Rendering and correctness depend on the content the model produces.

fixes.problem: I see broken content or plain markup
fixes.solution: Ask the assistant to regenerate a supported self-contained visual. For a complex interface or package-dependent project, continue in Code.

lessons.keywords: mock mocking module mockup design chart graph diagram interactive widget HTML SVG calculator
lessons.example: Show me an interactive study timer mockup. Let me change the session length. Keep it self-contained and easy to use.

lessons.title: Continue an idea in Code
lessons.summary: Turn a conversation into project work with the right context.
lessons.location: Chat → Continue in Code / handoff card when offered.
before: Have an idea or useful answer in Chat.
Choose a workspace for the Code work.

steps.title: Describe what should be built
steps.body: Ask to continue the idea in Code. Chat may also offer a handoff when your request needs file changes or commands.

steps.title: Review the handoff
steps.body: Read the proposed task/context and choose the workspace that should receive the work. Confirm any choices shown by the handoff flow.

steps.title: Check the Code conversation
steps.body: Once it opens, verify the selected workspace and model. Add any constraints that were missing, such as language, testing, or files to avoid.

steps.title: Review and test the implementation
steps.body: Use the Code activity, file changes, and project checks to inspect what actually changed. Return to the original Chat when you want to discuss the idea further.

lessons.outcome: The Code side has the task context needed to work on the chosen project.
limits: A handoff does not prove the task has been implemented. The Code run still needs to complete and be checked.
Chat itself does not gain workspace editing or shell tools after offering a handoff.

fixes.solution: Stop before edits, choose the correct workspace, and restate where the work belongs.

lessons.title: Work with replies and versions
lessons.summary: Quote a passage, retry an answer, or branch the conversation.
lessons.location: A conversation → message actions or selected text.
before: Have a saved conversation with at least one reply.

steps.title: Select the useful text
steps.body: Long-press/select a passage to copy it or quote it in a follow-up where the selection actions are available. A precise quote makes a correction easier to understand.

steps.title: Retry with a purpose
steps.body: Use Retry on the response you want to regenerate. Where offered, choose another model. Answer-version controls let you inspect or select the available alternatives.

steps.title: Fork at a turning point
steps.body: Use Fork from this message to create a separate conversation from that point. Give the branch a clear purpose so the original discussion stays useful.

steps.title: Save or share the result
steps.body: Use the answer’s save, copy, or sharing actions as available. Review the text and attachments before sending anything through Android’s share sheet.

lessons.outcome: You have a focused follow-up, an alternative reply, or a separate branch you can return to.
limits: A retry uses the selected provider again and can incur another charge.
A fork copies conversation context; it is not a separate copy of your project files. Code branches can still refer to the same workspace.

fixes.solution: Use the version controls when available to return to the preferred answer, or send a more specific follow-up instead of repeatedly retrying.

lessons.title: Find and organize conversations
lessons.summary: Keep useful chats and answers easy to return to.
lessons.location: Navigation menu → conversation lists, search, and saved answers.
before: Have one or more conversations saved in the app.

steps.title: Search for something you remember
steps.body: Use conversation search to find words from a title or message. In a conversation, use Find in chat to move between matching passages.

steps.title: Name and pin useful work
steps.body: Use the conversation’s menu or list actions to rename and pin it. Pinning makes important conversations easier to find.

steps.title: Archive finished topics
steps.body: Archive a conversation when you want it out of the active list but still available. Use the archived view to bring it back. Selection actions can manage multiple conversations where offered.

steps.title: Keep answers or remove old work
steps.body: Save useful replies to Saved answers. When deleting conversations, read the confirmation and the selected items; use a chat backup first if you need to keep the history.

lessons.outcome: You can reopen a conversation, find a passage, or return to a saved answer without recreating the task.
limits: Archiving and deleting are different actions. Do not use Delete when you only want to tidy the active list.
A conversation backup is separate from a backup of the files in its workspace.

fixes.problem: I cannot find an old conversation
fixes.solution: Search its content, check Chat versus Code and the selected project, then look in archived conversations.

lessons.title: Use the source library
lessons.summary: See which web pages appeared in a conversation.
lessons.location: Chat → conversation menu → Sources in this chat.
before: A conversation that has used web search or page-reading tools.

steps.title: Open Sources
steps.body: Use the conversation menu and open the source library. It gathers the web sources associated with this conversation.

steps.title: Distinguish discovery from reading
steps.body: A page found in search is not necessarily a page the assistant read. Look at the source’s status/label before relying on its details.

steps.title: Open the original
steps.body: Tap the link to inspect its date, author, and context. Return to the conversation to ask for a correction or comparison if needed.

lessons.outcome: You can trace a researched answer back to the pages it used or discovered.
limits: A source entry is not an endorsement of a website or proof that every sentence is supported.
The library is for the current conversation’s web sources, not all files and knowledge in the app.

fixes.solution: Ask a question using web research or provide a readable link; ordinary offline answers may have no web sources.

lessons.title: Create a personal Chat agent
lessons.summary: Give a study partner or writing companion its own setup.
lessons.location: A Chat’s settings, or Settings → Chat settings → Chat agents.
before: Know the agent’s purpose and the model it should use.

steps.title: Create the profile
steps.body: Choose Create agent. Set its name, icon, description, instructions, tone, and optional conversation starters.

steps.title: Choose model and knowledge
steps.body: Use the current Chat model or select a specific one. Add text, Markdown, or readable PDFs as knowledge. The editor shows the current file and character limits.

steps.title: Choose tools and memory
steps.body: Review web, image inspection, GitHub, history, memory scope, and instruction-based skills. Pick private agent memory, shared personal memory, or Off according to your goal.

steps.title: Save and start a conversation
steps.body: Save the agent, then start a new conversation from its profile. Edit or duplicate it later when you want another version.

lessons.outcome: A new conversation starts with the selected agent’s saved identity, instructions, model, and permitted Chat tools.
limits: Profile edits apply to new conversations. Existing conversations keep the agent setup they saved when they started.
Knowledge passages are searched locally and relevant text can be supplied to your chosen model. Scanned PDFs need text recognition; Chat agents remain within Chat capabilities.

fixes.problem: An agent ignores a knowledge file
fixes.solution: Check that the file imported readable text, ask a question about a specific section, and confirm that the chosen model has enough context.

lessons.keywords: study writing tutor modules knowledge personal assistant

lessons.title: Personalize one Chat or all Chats
lessons.summary: Set instructions, memory use, pictures, and thinking visibility.
lessons.location: Settings → Chat settings; a Chat → Chat settings or personalization control.
before: Decide whether the preference belongs to every Chat or just this one.

steps.title: Set app-wide Chat preferences
steps.body: In Chat settings, set general instructions, how often pictures should be added, and whether thinking starts collapsed. These are defaults for ordinary Chat behavior.

steps.title: Override one conversation
steps.body: Open Chat settings. Keep global instructions or replace them for this Chat. The image-frequency choice can follow the app setting or override it here.

steps.title: Review personalization
steps.body: Turn personalization off when you do not want this Chat to use its saved instructions and memory. The saved instruction text is retained so you can turn it back on later.

steps.title: Check the effect in a new request
steps.body: Save and send a follow-up that exercises the preference. If an agent profile is active, also review its saved setup and permissions.

lessons.outcome: The next request uses the instructions and personalization choices appropriate to this Chat.
limits: These preferences influence the assistant’s requests; they cannot force a model to support unavailable features or produce a correct answer.
Setting pictures to None suppresses response images. It does not turn a text-only model into an image-capable one.

fixes.problem: My global instructions are missing here
fixes.solution: Check whether this Chat replaces them, personalization is off, or an agent profile supplies its own instructions.

lessons.title: Remember useful facts and manage them
lessons.summary: Keep preferences and project context under your control.
lessons.location: Settings → Memory; project-specific memory is also available from a project.
before: Enable the memory features you want to use. Never use memory as a password store.

steps.title: Choose the scope
steps.body: In Memory settings, review the main switch, Chat and Code memory, and cross-section recall. Agent profiles can also have private or shared memory rules.

steps.title: Ask to remember or recall
steps.body: Tell the assistant what to remember and whether it is personal or about the current project. Ask what it remembers when you want to inspect the stored context.

steps.title: Review the manager
steps.body: Search and filter entries. Add, edit, enable/disable, or pin a fact. Use the consolidation controls when you want to review merged or overlapping memories.

steps.title: Correct or remove a memory
steps.body: Edit an inaccurate entry or ask to forget it, then check the manager. Use Clear only after reviewing the scope and confirmation.

lessons.outcome: The manager shows the facts you chose to keep, and relevant enabled memories can be used in later requests.
limits: Memory is selective context, not a complete transcript or guaranteed recall of every past chat.
Relevant saved text is supplied to the selected model when used. Disabling memory and deleting saved history are separate actions.

fixes.problem: A memory is not being used
fixes.solution: Check the main switch, section switches, project/agent scope, entry state, and this Chat’s personalization setting.

lessons.title: Speak a message and hear replies
lessons.summary: Set up voice input and speech output independently.
lessons.location: Settings → Voice & speech; conversation → microphone and reply speech controls.
before: Grant microphone permission when Android asks.
Groq speech needs its own key in Voice & speech and an internet connection.

steps.title: Choose voice input
steps.body: Select the system speech option or Groq/Whisper as offered. For Groq, paste a key in this page’s key field, verify/save it, and choose an available transcription model.

steps.title: Record deliberately
steps.body: Use the microphone beside the message box. Follow the visible recording controls to stop, lock, send, or discard the recording. Review the transcribed text before sending when it is placed in the draft.

steps.title: Choose speech output
steps.body: Pick the system text-to-speech engine or an available Groq speech model/voice. Select a voice and speed, then use Test voice. Some cloud voices require accepting their provider terms.

steps.title: Read a reply aloud
steps.body: Use the reply’s speech control, or the automatic speaking preference if enabled. Stop playback when you are finished.

lessons.outcome: Your speech becomes usable message text, and the selected output voice can read a reply.
limits: System speech availability depends on installed Android services and language data. It is not guaranteed to work offline.
Cloud transcription and speech send the relevant audio/text to the provider and may be metered. This is not a guaranteed continuous realtime voice call.

fixes.solution: Test the voice in Settings, check the selected engine/key/model and any terms prompt, or choose an installed system voice.

lessons.title: Plan out loud with Live Mode
lessons.summary: Talk through an idea hands-free while a fast model answers out loud. Experimental.
lessons.location: Settings → Live Mode; conversation → the Live Mode button on an empty message box, or the + menu.
before: Turn on Live Mode in Settings. It is experimental and off by default.
Grant microphone permission when Android asks. Groq Whisper also needs a Groq key in Voice & speech.

steps.title: Pick a fast model
steps.body: In Settings → Live Mode, choose a light model for spoken replies, or keep the chat's model. The main agent keeps its own model, so a running task is not affected.

steps.title: Choose what it may do
steps.body: Talk only uses no tools. Read only can look at files to answer. Read and start tasks can also hand a plan to the main agent when you say go ahead, and the agent then works with the chat's usual permissions.

steps.title: Start talking
steps.body: Open Live Mode from the empty message box or the + menu and speak. There is no send button: when you stop talking it answers out loud, then listens again. Tap the orb to interrupt a reply, or use pause when you need quiet.

steps.title: Use the conversation later
steps.body: Each Live session is saved to the chat as one collapsible card. The agent reads it with the rest of the chat, so you can say "build what we planned" without repeating yourself.

lessons.outcome: A spoken planning session the agent can see in the chat, and optionally a task handed to the main agent.
limits: This is an early, experimental feature. Noisy rooms, long pauses and some speech engines can cut you off or mishear words.
While a task is running, the saved conversation waits until the task finishes, so it never interrupts the agent mid-step.
Live Mode pauses when the app goes to the background.

fixes.solution: Raise Pause before replying in Settings → Live Mode.
Check microphone permission and the speech-to-text engine in Voice & speech. Try Groq Whisper if the system recognizer is missing.

lessons.keywords: live mode hands free voice conversation talk planning realtime

lessons.title: Ask the assistant to adjust app settings
lessons.summary: Use plain language and review the change receipt.
lessons.location: Settings → Coding → Agent behavior → app-settings access; then Chat or Code.
before: Choose whether app-setting changes are Off, Ask first, or Allowed in the app-settings access control.

steps.title: Set the access preference
steps.body: Open Agent behavior and find app-settings access. Read the three choices and choose how much control you want the assistant to have.

steps.title: Ask for a specific change
steps.body: For example, ask for dark mode or a quieter haptic strength. The assistant can find supported controls and propose or make a permitted change.

steps.title: Review any approval
steps.body: Sensitive changes still need approval. Read the proposed before/after values. The assistant cannot enter your API keys or grant Android permissions for you.

steps.title: Check the receipt
steps.body: A settings-change card shows what changed and any steps you still need to take. Open the linked setting to verify or adjust it yourself.

lessons.outcome: A supported preference changes with a visible receipt, or the assistant explains the manual step required.
limits: Only the exposed settings catalogue is editable; not every app setting is an assistant tool.
Off disables these changes. Approval mode and sensitive-setting rules still apply when relevant.

fixes.problem: The assistant asks me to do it manually
fixes.solution: The control may require a secret, account sign-in, OS permission, authentication, or an action that the catalogue does not expose.

lessons.example: Switch the app to dark mode and show me what changed.

lessons.title: Choose and download a local model
lessons.summary: Start with a model your phone has room to run.
lessons.location: Settings → Local models → Explore.
before: A supported device architecture, enough free storage, and available RAM.
Internet access for the first download.

steps.title: Check your device
steps.body: Open the local-model device information and read the memory/storage estimates. A smaller quantized model is easier to try than the largest available download.

steps.title: Browse Explore
steps.body: Use recommended models or Hugging Face search. Choose the format and read the model details, licence, estimated resources, and compatibility notices.

steps.title: Download and wait
steps.body: Start the download and accept the resource notice if you intend to proceed. Track it in My models. A paused transfer can be resumed; discarding it removes its partial files.

steps.title: Load it for a conversation
steps.body: After installation, use the model’s select/load action. Wait for loading to finish, then choose the local model in a conversation and send a short message.

lessons.outcome: The model appears in My models and can answer locally after it is loaded.
limits: Installed files still need to be loaded into memory. Download size alone does not tell you the RAM required.
Local inference can work offline after setup, but web search, downloads, external providers, and connected services still need their own connections.

fixes.problem: The model downloads but cannot load
fixes.solution: Close memory-heavy apps, lower context/reply limits, or choose a smaller compatible model. Read the resource warning instead of repeatedly retrying.

lessons.title: Add a model from a Hugging Face link
lessons.summary: Import a compatible model that is not in the recommendations.
lessons.location: Settings → Local models → Explore → add model link.
before: A public supported model/repository link and its licence.
Enough space for downloads and any conversion working files.

steps.title: Choose the format first
steps.body: Choose GGUF for a compatible quantized GGUF model. Choose Safetensors only for an architecture the importer can handle with its configuration and tokenizer files.

steps.title: Paste the link
steps.body: Open the link-import action and paste a Hugging Face model page or a supported direct model-file link. Let the app check the available files.

steps.title: Choose the intended variant
steps.body: For GGUF, select the actual model weights and quantization you want. A vision projector is a companion file, not the main language model. Read the resource fit indicator.

steps.title: Download and load
steps.body: Confirm the import/download, wait for validation and any conversion to finish, then find the model in My models and load it.

lessons.outcome: A custom model entry is installed and available to load if its format and architecture are supported.
limits: A repository containing weights is not proof that the app can run that architecture. Gated/private downloads may require access the import flow does not provide.
Safetensors import can involve conversion; it is not a promise of native execution for every model format.

fixes.solution: Check the link and format, choose the correct repository/file, or use a supported GGUF variant instead.

lessons.keywords: modules local modules weights huggingface model link import

lessons.title: Import GGUF or Safetensors from your files
lessons.summary: Use model files you already downloaded.
lessons.location: Settings → Local models → Explore → import from files.
before: For GGUF, a complete main .gguf file.
For Safetensors, the model folder with all required weights, config, and tokenizer files.

steps.title: Pick the correct import action
steps.body: Choose GGUF or Safetensors in Explore and use its file/folder import control. Android opens a system picker.

steps.title: Grant the intended file access
steps.body: For GGUF, pick the model weights file. For Safetensors, choose the whole model folder so configuration, tokenizer, and every needed shard can be inspected.

steps.title: Wait for copying and checks
steps.body: The app copies the required content into model storage and checks resources. Safetensors may need conversion before it can be installed. Keep enough free space for this work.

steps.title: Open My models
steps.body: Find the imported entry, review its settings/details, and load it. Keep the original licence information with your source files.

lessons.outcome: A supported import appears as a custom local model and can be loaded.
limits: Picking one Safetensors shard without the rest of the model folder is insufficient.
ONNX, arbitrary ZIP packages, LoRA adapters, APK modules, and unrelated files are not interchangeable with a supported main model.

fixes.problem: Import reports missing files or unsupported architecture
fixes.solution: Supply the complete original model folder, or choose a supported GGUF model. Renaming a file extension does not convert a model.

lessons.keywords: local module modules import safetensors gguf offline files

lessons.title: Tune local context, replies, and thinking
lessons.summary: Balance useful context against memory, time, and heat.
lessons.location: Settings → Local models → My models → model settings.
before: Have a compatible model installed.

steps.title: Set conversation and reply size
steps.body: Choose the context size and reply length in tokens. Start modestly; larger context needs more memory and can make prompt processing slower.

steps.title: Choose thinking behavior
steps.body: Use Auto, Thinking, or Direct as offered. Auto follows the request; the model/template must still support the desired behavior.

steps.title: Open advanced settings only as needed
steps.body: Adjust the input budget, generation threads, and prompt threads. More threads are not always faster and can increase heat.

steps.title: Save and compare
steps.body: Save, load/reload the model as required, and try the same short prompt. Use Reset defaults if your changes make behavior worse.

lessons.outcome: The model uses your saved limits on subsequent loads/requests, within the runtime’s supported bounds.
limits: Thinking controls cannot reliably add or remove a reasoning capability absent from the model/template.
A large advertised model context does not mean your phone has enough memory to use all of it.

fixes.problem: Replies are very short or loading fails
fixes.solution: Check output/input/context budgets, reduce memory-heavy values, and retry a simple prompt. Use the performance page to measure instead of guessing.

lessons.title: CPU, GPU, and real performance
lessons.summary: Measure the device before choosing an acceleration setting.
lessons.location: Settings → Local models → Performance; model settings for processor choice.
before: An installed compatible local model.
Experimental local-model features enabled if you want the GPU controls.

steps.title: Read the live dashboard
steps.body: Open Performance to inspect the available device/RAM, processor, and thermal information. Some devices do not expose every reading.

steps.title: Enable experimental controls deliberately
steps.body: Use the experimental local-model switch and read its notice. If GPU support needs the optional runtime, use the installer offered by the app and wait for verification.

steps.title: Choose CPU, GPU, or Auto
steps.body: Use the model’s Processor control. Auto prefers a supported GPU and can fall back to CPU when GPU startup is unavailable. A GPU label is not proof of better speed.

steps.title: Run a comparison
steps.body: Use the benchmark controls for CPU, GPU, or both when available. Compare prompt processing and generation, inspect the results, and apply the settings you actually want.

lessons.outcome: You have measured results for the selected model/device and a saved processor/thread choice.
limits: Vulkan GPU support depends on device drivers, architecture, build, and runtime availability. GPU can be slower or less stable than CPU.
Benchmarks create heat and use battery. Performance changes with model size, context, temperature, and other running apps.

fixes.solution: Read the reported reason, check the optional runtime installation, and choose CPU. Report the device/build details if you can reproduce a GPU failure.

lessons.title: Give a compatible local model image support
lessons.summary: Use the matching vision companion file when required.
lessons.location: Settings → Local models → custom model → Image support.
before: A vision-capable model supported by the local runtime.
A supported download link for the matching vision projector/mmproj .gguf file for that exact model.

steps.title: Check compatibility
steps.body: Read the model’s original documentation. A text-only model cannot understand images just because a projector file is present.

steps.title: Open Image support
steps.body: Use the custom model’s Image support control. Paste the matching projector’s download link in Vision file link (.gguf); this dialog downloads the companion rather than opening a local-file picker.

steps.title: Install the companion
steps.body: Choose Add vision file and wait for the download and checks to finish. The projector adds storage and memory requirements.

steps.title: Test a simple image
steps.body: Load/select the model, attach a clear small image, and ask one question about it. Confirm that the app/provider reports image support.

lessons.outcome: A supported vision model can receive image input with its installed companion files.
limits: Projectors must match their base model and runtime. Arbitrary mmproj files are not universal adapters.
Image processing costs memory and time; not all local architectures or image tasks are supported.

fixes.problem: The image is rejected or the reply is nonsense
fixes.solution: Check the model/projector match and runtime support, reduce input size if appropriate, or use another image-capable model.

lessons.title: Stop, unload, resume, or remove a model
lessons.summary: Understand which action frees memory and which frees storage.
lessons.location: Settings → Local models → My models and Options.
before: Wait for or stop any request using the model before changing it.

steps.title: Stop and unload to free RAM
steps.body: Use the model’s stop/unload control and wait for it to finish. The downloaded files remain installed so you can load them again later.

steps.title: Resume a paused download
steps.body: Find the paused transfer and choose Resume. Discard removes the partial content when you no longer want that download.

steps.title: Remove to free storage
steps.body: Use Remove/uninstall on the model you no longer need and read the confirmation. You will need to import/download it again to use it later.

steps.title: Review storage and options
steps.body: Use local-model storage controls for paused files or leftovers. Options also contains the system/tools-context preference; enabling that adds context and is not proof that a small model can use tools reliably.

lessons.outcome: You can reclaim RAM, resume a transfer, or remove model storage using the intended action.
limits: Stopping generation and unloading model memory are different from deleting the installed weights.
Local model binaries are excluded from settings backups; back up or keep your original source files separately.

fixes.problem: The phone still feels memory constrained
fixes.solution: Wait for unloading, close other memory-heavy apps, and review the device memory display. Choose a smaller model/context on the next load.

lessons.title: Choose the right workspace
lessons.summary: Give Code a clear home for files and commands.
lessons.location: Code → workspace selector, or navigation menu → Projects → add workspace.
before: Know which folder or repository belongs to the task.

steps.title: Use an app workspace for a simple start
steps.body: The private app workspace is a convenient place for new experiments and shell-based projects. Other apps do not automatically see these files.

steps.title: Choose an existing device folder when needed
steps.body: Browse device folders for a directly accessible path, or use System picker to grant a selected folder without broad storage access. Check the shown path and access state.

steps.title: Use GitHub or SSH for other sources
steps.body: Import a GitHub repository into a workspace, or connect to an SSH host. These are separate choices with their own connection requirements.

steps.title: Confirm the active workspace
steps.body: Select the workspace in Code before asking for edits. Use its Files screen to check that the expected project files are present.

lessons.outcome: Code is working against the intended folder, and you can identify its path and access type.
limits: System-picker file access does not automatically provide the direct shell path needed by every build or command.
A workspace is a folder, not an automatic backup or isolation from every other chat using that same folder.

fixes.problem: Files work but commands do not
fixes.solution: Check the workspace type and shell-path support. Use an app/direct-path workspace or a properly connected SSH workspace for command-based projects.

lessons.title: Organize and remove projects
lessons.summary: See a project’s chats, files, checks, and automation in one place.
lessons.location: Navigation menu → Projects → choose a project.
before: Have a workspace added to the app.

steps.title: Open the project overview
steps.body: Choose the project and inspect its path, recent conversations, file shortcuts, checks, memory, and automation controls as available.

steps.title: Start work in the right context
steps.body: Open or create a Code conversation from that project. Use the project’s Files, Terminal, or checks action when you want to work directly.

steps.title: Keep instructions with the project
steps.body: Use project memory/instructions for context that belongs to this project rather than to every Chat.

steps.title: Remove a project carefully
steps.body: Use the project removal action only after reading its confirmation and data choices. Back up important conversations and files before choosing any option that deletes them.

lessons.outcome: Your work is associated with the intended project, and its related tools are easy to reopen.
limits: Removing an app entry and deleting project data have different consequences. Follow the specific choices shown in the confirmation.
Running tasks and unavailable storage can prevent a safe removal; resolve those conditions before retrying.

fixes.solution: Stop tasks using it and read the failure message. Do not manually delete app-private directories to bypass a blocked removal.

lessons.title: Use several workspaces in one Code chat
lessons.summary: Let one task compare or coordinate selected projects.
lessons.location: Code → workspace selector → Workspaces for this chat.
before: Add each project to AndroidHarness first.
Pause active work before changing the conversation’s file access.

steps.title: Choose the projects
steps.body: Open Workspaces for this chat and select only the projects the task needs.

steps.title: Set access for each
steps.body: Choose Read only or Can edit per workspace. Pick the Primary workspace; it is the default destination for new files.

steps.title: Save and name the task boundaries
steps.body: Save the selection, then tell the assistant which project each part belongs to. Check the workspace context before approving edits.

steps.title: Use file tools within the grants
steps.body: The assistant can read the selected projects and edit the ones granted edit access. Review every affected project after a cross-project change.

lessons.outcome: The conversation has explicit per-project access and a clear primary workspace.
limits: Commands and integrations require edit access to all selected workspaces.
Workspace MCP servers are not available in multi-workspace chats yet. Per-workspace access still matters even if another chat can edit that folder.

fixes.solution: Review the access warning in the sheet. Use a single workspace or grant the required edit access only when appropriate.

lessons.title: Work on an SSH host
lessons.summary: Use a remote folder while the project and commands stay on its server.
lessons.location: Add workspace → Connect through SSH.
before: A reachable SSH server, its login details, and a folder you can access.
Verify the server identity before trusting a new host key.

steps.title: Enter the connection
steps.body: Supply the host, port, username, and the authentication offered by the dialog. Choose the intended remote folder.

steps.title: Test and verify
steps.body: Use the connection/probe controls. Review the host identity/fingerprint and any failure before saving a connection.

steps.title: Open the remote workspace
steps.body: Select it in Code or Files. Commands and file actions use that remote context; check the workspace label before running anything.

steps.title: Plan for interruptions
steps.body: Keep the network and host available. If the connection drops, inspect the run/job state before retrying a command that may already have started.

lessons.outcome: The remote folder appears as a workspace and supported actions operate on the SSH host.
limits: A remote server’s localhost is not your phone’s localhost. Remote web previews need a URL reachable from the phone or a separately configured connection.
AndroidHarness does not install or administer the remote SSH server for you.

fixes.solution: Check the host/port, credentials, allowed authentication, remote folder permissions, and network. A changed host key needs investigation rather than blind acceptance.

lessons.title: Browse and edit project files
lessons.summary: Make a direct edit and know when it has been saved.
lessons.location: Navigation menu → Files, or a project’s Files action.
before: Choose a readable workspace. Editing also needs write access.

steps.title: Find the file
steps.body: Browse folders or use Quick Open. File actions let you create, rename, move/copy, or remove items as supported by the current workspace. Review the destination for multi-file operations.

steps.title: Open and edit
steps.body: Tap a text file to open the editor. Use its tabs to switch between open files. Unsaved drafts are marked so you can tell them apart from content saved on disk.

steps.title: Save deliberately
steps.body: Use Save or Ctrl+S with a keyboard. When leaving a dirty editor, use the save/discard decision shown. If the file changed elsewhere, review the conflict before overwriting.

steps.title: Ask for help with context
steps.body: Use the selected-code/Ask agent actions for a focused question or edit. Check the resulting draft/diff and save the changes you intend to keep.

lessons.outcome: Your edit is saved in the chosen workspace and can be reopened from Files.
limits: Draft recovery helps after interruptions but is not a replacement for saving and backing up important files.
Binary, very large, unsupported, or read-only files may be previewed differently or not editable.

fixes.problem: The editor shows an external-change conflict
fixes.solution: Compare the on-disk version with your draft, decide what to keep, and use the editor’s offered conflict action. Do not assume another chat’s edit is already in your draft.

lessons.title: Quick Open and search across a project
lessons.summary: Find files or text and review replacements before applying them.
lessons.location: Files or editor → workspace tools → Files / Search / Commands.
before: A selected workspace with readable files.

steps.title: Use Quick Open for a path
steps.body: Open Files in workspace tools and type part of a file name or path. With a keyboard, Ctrl+P opens Quick Open.

steps.title: Search file contents
steps.body: Choose Search, enter the text, and use case, regular-expression, include, or exclude filters as needed. Ctrl+Shift+F opens project search.

steps.title: Review a replacement
steps.body: Open Replace, enter the replacement, and review the proposed changes. Select the files you actually want to update before applying.

steps.title: Use the command palette
steps.body: Choose Commands or Ctrl+Shift+P to find editor/project actions without hunting through menus.

lessons.outcome: You can jump to matching content and apply reviewed replacements to the intended files.
limits: Search skips some binary, large, unreadable, or excluded files and caps large result sets. Narrow the query before replacing.
Replacement can be blocked by active agent work, unsaved drafts, or a changed workspace. Resolve the stated condition and review again.

fixes.solution: Check the expression and capture groups. Start with plain text and add filters gradually; review every replacement before applying it.

lessons.title: Outline, format, definitions, and rename
lessons.summary: Use language-aware editor actions where the file supports them.
lessons.location: Editor → code tools or command palette.
before: Open a supported source file in the editor.
Wait for the editor to finish reading its language/project symbols.

steps.title: Navigate the document
steps.body: Use Code outline to jump to a function, class, or document symbol. Find and Go to line help with a known location.

steps.title: Follow a symbol
steps.body: Place the cursor on a symbol and use Go to Definition or Find References when offered. Review the returned project locations.

steps.title: Format the draft
steps.body: Use Format Document for a supported language. Inspect the draft and undo the formatting if it is not what you intended.

steps.title: Rename with review
steps.body: Choose Rename Symbol, enter the new name, and review affected files. The changes open as drafts; save each intended file after checking it.

lessons.outcome: You can navigate or make a supported language-aware change with visible drafts to review.
limits: Language actions depend on the file type and available project information. They are not a full desktop IDE for every language.
A semantic rename is different from a plain-text replacement; neither should be accepted without reviewing the affected files.

fixes.problem: The file changed while the sheet was open
fixes.solution: Close and reopen the code tools so the action uses the current document, then review again.

lessons.title: Review and undo file changes
lessons.summary: Understand the difference between a diff, file history, and Git.
lessons.location: Code → Files changed / change cards; conversation menu → Undo file changes.
before: Pause active tasks before undoing files.
Keep a separate backup or Git commit for important work.

steps.title: Read the diff
steps.body: Open the conversation’s changed files or a change card. Compare original and updated content; use sections to inspect a smaller part of a large diff.

steps.title: Ask about the change
steps.body: Use Ask about this file/section for an explanation tied to the shown diff. Open the actual file when you need to inspect its current contents.

steps.title: Undo the intended scope
steps.body: Use Undo file or Undo section where offered, and read its confirmation. Conversation-level undo/checkpoints and file-history tools can restore tracked content at their supported scope.

steps.title: Verify after restoring
steps.body: Reopen the file and run checks. Use Git separately when you want repository commits, branches, or remote publication.

lessons.outcome: You have inspected the actual edits and can restore a supported tracked change without deleting the chat history.
limits: Tracking can omit oversized pre-change content. A diff being unavailable does not mean the file was unchanged.
History/checkpoints cannot guarantee recovery of every external command’s side effect, deleted external data, remote publication, or unrelated changes.

fixes.solution: Stop tasks using the workspace, check access, and read the error. Inspect current content before trying another restore.

lessons.title: Plan before you act
lessons.summary: Inspect first, then explicitly move into implementation.
lessons.location: Code → Plan / Act control in the header.
before: Select the intended model and workspace.

steps.title: Choose Plan
steps.body: Ask the assistant to inspect the project, identify the relevant files, and propose a specific approach. Plan mode restricts the run to inspection-oriented work.

steps.title: Read the proposal
steps.body: Look for assumptions, prerequisites, and how the result will be checked. Correct the plan before asking for implementation.

steps.title: Switch to Act
steps.body: Choose Act when you want permitted tools to make changes. If separate planning/execution models are enabled, check the model for the new role.

steps.title: Review the work
steps.body: Follow approvals, changes, and test results. Switch back to Plan for another inspection if the scope changes.

lessons.outcome: You have a reviewed approach followed by an Act run when you are ready to apply it.
limits: Plan mode is a tool policy, not a substitute for reading the proposed actions or results.
Act can only do what the selected model, tools, workspace access, and permissions allow.

fixes.problem: No files changed after a planning answer
fixes.solution: Select Act and give the implementation request. A plan response is not an applied patch.

lessons.title: Steer, queue, pause, and resume a task
lessons.summary: Keep control while the assistant is already working.
lessons.location: A running conversation → composer, task controls, activity, and Context & limits.
before: Know which task is running before sending new instructions.

steps.title: Send a correction while it works
steps.body: Type a short steering message. The active steering preference determines whether it is read at the next step or queued until the task finishes.

steps.title: Manage the queue
steps.body: Open Manage queue to edit, reorder, remove, or send a queued message now when offered. A queued message is waiting work, not a completed instruction.

steps.title: Ask a side question
steps.body: Use the side-question control or /btw where offered for a brief question alongside the task. Check its separate response instead of assuming it rewrote the main task.

steps.title: Pause or stop intentionally
steps.body: Use the visible task controls. After an interruption, review saved progress and Resume task when appropriate. Inspect any command that was in flight before retrying.

lessons.outcome: Your next instruction has a clear place in the task, and you can stop or continue work deliberately.
limits: Steering is read at supported boundaries; it cannot undo an action that already happened.
Auto-continue has a saved retry limit. It does not guarantee recovery or safely repeat every side effect.

fixes.solution: Check Manage queue and the steering mode. It may be waiting until the current task sends its finished notification.

lessons.title: Context, budgets, and recovery
lessons.summary: Control how much a task can consume and retain.
lessons.location: Conversation menu → Context & limits; Settings → Coding → Agent behavior for defaults.
before: Pause the task before editing task-level controls when the screen asks you to.

steps.title: Inspect context and usage
steps.body: Open Context & limits to see the available context/usage display. Context is the information sent to the model, not the entire visible conversation history.

steps.title: Keep the important instructions
steps.body: Use pinned instructions and review the saved summary. Removing older context keeps the supported recent turn/summary/pins while leaving visible chat history in place.

steps.title: Set optional task budgets
steps.body: Enter total token, estimated cost, or active-time limits if you need them. Leave a field blank for unlimited. Task-wide usage includes subagents where tracked.

steps.title: Set recovery behavior
steps.body: Choose auto-continue and its retry limit. For general defaults, review maximum context and tool-iteration settings under Agent behavior.

lessons.outcome: The task has the context, budget, and retry settings you chose, with saved changes visible in its controls.
limits: Estimates depend on available provider pricing and usage metadata; they are not a provider-enforced spending cap.
Compaction and context removal can lose useful detail. Preserve essential decisions in pins or a clear summary.

fixes.problem: The task stops at a limit
fixes.solution: Review its usage and saved state, then raise the intended limit or narrow the task before resuming. Avoid repeatedly continuing without checking the cause.

lessons.title: Understand approvals and Full access
lessons.summary: Choose the level of supervision deliberately.
lessons.location: Settings → Coding → Agent behavior; Code header → permission control.
before: Read the action preview before approving a tool.
Device/root access is separate from the agent approval mode.

steps.title: Choose a default mode
steps.body: Confirm everything asks for every approval-eligible action. Confirm risky actions keeps targeted confirmations. Full auto reduces prompts while retaining its normal policy boundaries.

steps.title: Understand Full access
steps.body: Full access removes the agent’s normal approval, shell denylist, and path-containment layers. The app asks for device authentication when enabling sensitive access where required.

steps.title: Read each prompt you receive
steps.body: Check the command, diff, target, and scope. Use a one-time approval when the action is specific. Remembered/Always grants apply at their stated command/tool and workspace scope.

steps.title: Review remembered permissions
steps.body: Open workspace access settings to inspect and revoke saved grants. Return to a more supervised mode whenever the task does not need broad access.

lessons.outcome: The assistant runs with the permission mode and saved grants you actually intended.
limits: Full access cannot grant Android OS permissions, root, a remote account role, or unavailable provider capabilities.
Disabling confirmations increases what can happen without another prompt. Use a workspace and backups appropriate to that choice.

fixes.problem: An action still asks in an automatic mode
fixes.solution: Sensitive settings, device/root decisions, workspace trust, or OS permissions can require their own decision. Read the specific prompt instead of repeatedly changing modes.

lessons.title: Build, test, and ask the agent to fix a failure
lessons.summary: Run the project’s real checks and inspect their output.
lessons.location: Project → Project checks / Build & Test, or the workspace’s check action.
before: A workspace with a usable shell path.
The project’s required runtime, packages, SDK, and build files.

steps.title: Choose a check
steps.body: Open Build & Test. Use a suggested/saved command or Add command with a name and the actual test/build command for this project.

steps.title: Run and inspect
steps.body: Run the check and watch live output. Read the exit code and error list. Stop a command that is stuck or doing the wrong work.

steps.title: Use Fix with agent
steps.body: For a failure, choose the fix action. The failed command and recent output are sent to a fresh agent chat; review its task and workspace before it changes files.

steps.title: Run the check again
