steps.body: After the fix, rerun the same command and inspect the result. Use Run & preview separately when you want to launch a supported project server or HTML preview.

lessons.outcome: You have an actual command result, and any fix can be checked with the same command.
limits: A successful build does not prove all functionality works. Exercise the feature that changed.
Unsupported desktop binaries, unavailable SDK components, remote access, or Android restrictions can prevent a project from building here.

fixes.solution: Add the command from the project’s build/test setup. If the workspace lacks a direct shell path, move/copy the project to a suitable workspace first.

lessons.title: Use the Terminal
lessons.summary: Run commands yourself in the selected workspace, including full-screen programs such as nano and fzf.
lessons.location: Navigation menu → Terminal, or a project/editor terminal action.
before: Know whether this is an app/device shell or an SSH workspace.
Have the required command/package installed. Install the Linux environment to get bash and packages.

steps.title: Check the workspace and mode
steps.body: Read the header before typing. In a local workspace the Terminal opens in interactive mode: a live bash shell running as the app user, with the current folder under the title. The terminal button beside the title switches to command mode, which follows the access mode (Shizuku, Wireless ADB or root) and is the only mode for SSH workspaces.

steps.title: Type into the live shell
steps.body: Tap the terminal to bring up the keyboard and type as you would on a computer. Keys go straight to the running program, so nano, fzf, Python, top and interactive prompts work. Pinch to change the text size, scroll up to read earlier output, and long-press to paste.

steps.title: Use the extra keys
steps.body: The two rows above the keyboard add Esc, Tab, arrows, Home, End, Page Up and Page Down, plus a Ctrl+C key. Tap Ctrl or Alt once to apply it to the next key, or twice to keep it on until you tap it again. Fn shows F1 to F12, Insert, Delete and common symbols. A hardware keyboard works too, with Ctrl+Shift+V to paste and Ctrl+Shift+C to copy.

steps.title: Stop or restart
steps.body: Press the Ctrl+C key to interrupt the running program. The ⋮ menu has Paste, Copy output, Reset text size and Restart shell. The shell keeps running when you leave the screen or rotate the phone. In command mode, enter a command and tap Run, and use Stop for the active command.

steps.title: Use Code for an assisted task
steps.body: Return to Code if you want the assistant to inspect output, edit files, or coordinate several commands. Include the exact error and what you expected.

lessons.outcome: You can see the command’s real output in the intended environment and work with interactive programs directly.
limits: A terminal does not automatically grant root or access to protected folders. On a rooted device, running su in the interactive terminal gives a root shell.
Interactive mode runs in local workspaces as the app user. Shizuku, Wireless ADB, root routes and SSH workspaces use command mode.
Long lines are not re-wrapped when the terminal width changes; full-screen programs redraw themselves.
Fallback is chosen before a command starts. Interrupted commands are not automatically repeated on another access route.

fixes.solution: Install the relevant package in the environment that runs the command, or check the SSH host’s tools. Installing a phone package does not install it on the remote host.
The Linux environment is not installed, so the terminal uses Android’s own shell. Install it from Settings → Terminal & device → Linux environment, then choose Restart shell from the ⋮ menu.
Type exit in the interactive terminal first, because cleanup will not delete files a running shell may be using.

lessons.keywords: pty interactive shell bash nano fzf ctrl+c extra keys tui

lessons.title: Run and inspect a web preview
lessons.summary: Open local HTML, a dev server, or a reachable web page.
lessons.location: Code → web preview/browser control; Project checks → Run & preview.
before: A supported HTML project, a running development server, or a reachable URL.

steps.title: Choose the source
steps.body: Open Web & HTML Preview. Pick a workspace HTML file, a detected local server, a chat link, or enter an address/port. Rescan ports after starting a server.

steps.title: Run a project if needed
steps.body: Use Run & preview/Run project for a detected project script, or start the server from Terminal. Wait for the URL in the output before opening the preview.

steps.title: Inspect the page
steps.body: Use back/forward, reload, fullscreen, console, and the available developer tools. Open externally when you need your normal browser.

steps.title: Ask for a focused fix
steps.body: Use Select element to fix or the console’s fix action, describe the desired change, and send the captured page context to the agent. Review the resulting project edits.

lessons.outcome: The selected page renders and you can connect a visible problem with a Code task.
limits: A local server must keep running. HTTPS, authentication, remote-host URLs, WebView behavior, and network policy can affect loading.
Browser tool control is limited to the supported in-app browser tools; it is not arbitrary control of every app on the phone.

fixes.solution: Check the server output and port, verify the phone can reach the address, and confirm that a remote server is not being mistaken for phone localhost.

lessons.title: Create and save a visual concept in Code
lessons.summary: Make a self-contained interactive HTML concept you can reopen.
lessons.location: Code → ask for an interactive concept; open its result card in the conversation.
before: A Code model with the relevant artifact tools available.

steps.title: Describe the concept
steps.body: Ask for a UI mockup, chart, diagram, or small interactive tool as a self-contained HTML concept. Provide the real content or data it should show.

steps.title: Open the result card
steps.body: When creation succeeds, preview or expand the concept. Test its controls and use View source when you want to inspect the generated HTML.

steps.title: Revise or save it
steps.body: Ask for a change to this concept so the tool can use its existing identity/revision. Review the new preview, then use the card’s Save action if you want an exported copy.

lessons.outcome: The conversation contains a real concept card with its saved HTML content and available revisions.
limits: Concept previews have no network, file access, cookies, native bridge, popups, or permissions. Use inline HTML/CSS/JavaScript/SVG rather than external libraries or live service calls.
Creating a concept does not modify workspace files or build an installed app. Regular Chat uses its inline visual system; use Code file work for a real project with packages and services.

fixes.problem: The concept fails or needs external packages
fixes.solution: Ask for a supported self-contained HTML version, or ask Code to implement actual project files and use a project preview instead.

lessons.keywords: artifact concept saved HTML mockup diagram interactive revision export

lessons.title: Project instructions and project memory
lessons.summary: Give the assistant the context it should keep using.
lessons.location: Settings → Coding → Agent behavior → project instructions; Project → memory; Configuration for advanced setup.
before: Select the intended project before editing its instructions.

steps.title: Write practical instructions
steps.body: Use the project-instructions editor for conventions such as language, checks, and files to avoid. State a concrete rule and its reason when that helps.

steps.title: Keep project facts in project memory
steps.body: Record decisions and context that belong to this project. Review them when the project changes rather than accumulating stale notes.

steps.title: Use Configuration for larger setups
steps.body: For multiple instruction files, references, named agents, and project tools, use the Configuration page and inspect the effective configuration.

steps.title: Check the next request
steps.body: Start a focused task and confirm that the chosen workspace and intended instructions are being used. Correct stale instructions before asking for broad work.

lessons.outcome: The project’s recurring rules and useful context have a clear home.
limits: Instructions are model context, not a guarantee of compliance or a substitute for access controls.
Global, project, per-chat, and agent-profile instructions have different scopes. Avoid contradictory rules and use the effective configuration to inspect combined sources.

fixes.problem: The assistant follows an old convention
fixes.solution: Review project memory, instruction files, Configuration sources, and per-chat instructions for a conflicting rule.

lessons.title: Add and use a skill
lessons.summary: Give the assistant reusable instructions for a particular kind of work.
lessons.location: Settings → Coding → Skills; conversation → skill picker.
before: A skill is instructions and supporting material, not a model or Android module.

steps.title: Browse the existing skills
steps.body: Open Skills and review bundled, user, and workspace skills. Enable the ones you want the assistant to be able to discover.

steps.title: Create a user skill
steps.body: Choose Add skill and edit the supplied SKILL.md-style template. Keep its name, description, and instructions clear and specific. Save only when the editor accepts the format.

steps.title: Use the skill in a task
steps.body: Choose it from the conversation’s skill picker or ask for it by name. In Code, slash/skill commands can also load supported skills.

steps.title: Maintain the right source
steps.body: Edit or delete your own user skill from the manager. Workspace/plugin skills are managed at their source. Disable a skill when you do not want it offered.

lessons.outcome: The enabled skill is discoverable and can supply instructions when you invoke it.
limits: A skill does not install its required packages, create API access, or guarantee that a model follows every instruction.
Chat agents accept supported instruction-based skills with size limits. Skills requiring workspace edits or commands belong in Code.

fixes.solution: Check its enabled state, valid metadata, source/scope, and any Chat-specific size or capability restriction.

lessons.title: Use shortcuts and custom commands
lessons.summary: Run the supported conversation shortcuts or reuse a prompt.
lessons.location: Code → type /; Settings → Coding → Code conversation & commands for custom commands.
before: Choose a workspace before running Code-specific actions.

steps.title: See the available commands
steps.body: Type / and read the suggestions for the current screen. Built-in commands include context, cost, environment, doctor, initialization, planning, skills, and side-question helpers where supported.

steps.title: Use a context shortcut
steps.body: Use /compact to reduce older model context, /cost for usage information, or /env for environment help. Read the result before assuming an operation completed.

steps.title: Create a reusable prompt
steps.body: In the Coding chat/commands section, choose Add custom command, enter a short name and prompt, then save. Invoke it with /name.

steps.title: Treat powerful shortcuts as real work
steps.body: /init and /doctor can start agent tasks. Read their purpose, use an appropriate workspace, and review any tools/approvals they require.

lessons.outcome: You can invoke a supported shortcut or insert a saved prompt without retyping it.
limits: Some commands are Code-only or start model/tool work and can incur provider usage.
Clearing/compacting model context, deleting history, and undoing files are separate actions. Read the command’s actual behavior.

fixes.solution: Check the spelling and current suggestions. Make sure a custom command was saved with that name and that the current mode supports it.

lessons.title: Use subagents for separate parts of a task
lessons.summary: Delegate focused work and inspect each agent’s real result.
lessons.location: Settings → Coding → Sub-Agent settings; Code → subagent activity cards.
before: Use a tool-capable model and a task that can be divided clearly.

steps.title: Choose the subagent model
steps.body: Open the Subagent page and choose its provider/model. Review whether it inherits a default or uses your explicit selection.

steps.title: Choose tool and background access
steps.body: Review subagent action-tool access, background execution, and completion notifications. Background permission is not the same as permission to edit files or run commands.

steps.title: Ask for focused delegation
steps.body: Give each subtask a clear output and boundary. The main assistant can start delegates and use status/wait/stop controls when available.

steps.title: Inspect the result
steps.body: Open the subagent cards or detail screen for real status, activity, and answers. A stop request is not a completed result; check the final state.

lessons.outcome: Distinct subtasks have visible agent activity/results that can be incorporated into the main task.
limits: Subagents add model usage and share task-wide limits where tracked. Parallel work can still conflict in the same files.
A subagent can only use the allowed tools and workspace context; delegation does not grant extra account or device permissions.

fixes.solution: Check its activity and approvals, confirm background access/network, or stop that delegate and narrow the task.

lessons.title: Connect a remote MCP server
lessons.summary: Add a service’s tools to Code using its real endpoint.
lessons.location: Settings → Connected tools (MCP) → Add server.
before: Use the server operator’s trusted MCP configuration and account access.
MCP is a tool connection; it is different from a model provider API key.

steps.title: Paste the supplied configuration
steps.body: Add server accepts supported mcpServers JSON, a single-server definition, or a supported claude mcp add command. Paste the service’s own setup and read the server preview.

steps.title: Check transport and credentials
steps.body: For a remote server, use its Streamable HTTP endpoint or legacy SSE transport as documented. Add only its required static headers or use its supported sign-in flow.

steps.title: Save and test
steps.body: Save/enable the server and tap Test. A connected state and tool count confirm discovery. If it asks for authentication, finish the browser flow and test again.

steps.title: Use it from Code
steps.body: Ask for a specific action involving that service. Review any approval and the tool result. Disable, edit, or remove the server from the same settings page when needed.

lessons.outcome: The server reports connected tools that Code can call within the app’s tool policies.
limits: An ordinary website URL or REST endpoint is not necessarily an MCP endpoint.
Remote tools may read or change external data using the connected account. Chat’s built-in tool set does not automatically include every MCP tool.

fixes.problem: Connected but the tool is unavailable
fixes.solution: Check the server is enabled, the current Code/workspace configuration, account scope, and any trust/permission restrictions. For multi-workspace chats, review their MCP limitation.

lessons.keywords: MCP module modules integration connector mocking module server http sse oauth

lessons.title: Run a local MCP server
lessons.summary: Use stdio tools with the required runtime installed.
lessons.location: Settings → Connected tools (MCP) → Add server → paste or manual editor.
before: A trusted server that runs on the available Android/Linux environment.
Install the required runtime/packages before expecting its command to start.

steps.title: Read the server’s setup
steps.body: Identify its executable, arguments, environment variables, and any API key it requires. A copied desktop path may not exist on Android.

steps.title: Install the runtime if needed
steps.body: Prepare the optional Linux environment and packages such as Node or Python when the server needs them. Verify the executable from the app’s own command environment.

steps.title: Add the stdio configuration
steps.body: Paste the supported server configuration or use manual editing. Set command, arguments, and environment separately, then save and enable it.

steps.title: Test before using it
steps.body: Tap Test and inspect the connection/tool count or startup error. In Code, request one small read action before a larger workflow.

lessons.outcome: The executable starts as a local MCP process and advertises tools successfully.
limits: A local MCP server is executable software. AndroidHarness does not make arbitrary desktop binaries compatible with your phone.
Project-provided MCP/plugin configuration needs its workspace trust review. Workspace MCP is not available in multi-workspace chats yet.

fixes.problem: Executable not found or immediate exit
fixes.solution: Check runtime installation, command path, arguments, required environment variables, and architecture compatibility. Read the reported startup error.

lessons.title: Install and manage app plugins
lessons.summary: Review a bundle before enabling its skills, hooks, and tools.
lessons.location: Settings → Coding → Plugins → Installed / Discover / Add.
before: Use a plugin made for AndroidHarness’s supported bundle format.
Choose whether its scope should be this project or global.

steps.title: Find the bundle
steps.body: Use Discover, or Add from a supported npm package, GitHub repository, local archive, or folder. For GitHub, provide the correct ref/subfolder when required.

steps.title: Review the prepared contents
steps.body: Let the app read/download the bundle, then review its identity, contributions, hooks, and tool/configuration requirements before installing.

steps.title: Choose scope and install
steps.body: Choose project or global scope as offered. Confirm the reviewed bundle and complete any separate project-tool trust decision.

steps.title: Manage from Installed
steps.body: Filter the installed list by scope. Inspect details, enable/disable, update, or uninstall the bundle. Review update contents instead of assuming they are identical to the old version.

lessons.outcome: The installed plugin contributes its supported features in the scope you chose.
limits: An npm package or ZIP is not automatically a compatible plugin. A model, MCP definition, skill, APK, and plugin bundle are different things.
Executable hooks and MCP contributions can require a runtime and permissions; installing a bundle does not grant external service access.

fixes.solution: Check the format, manifest, selected ref/subfolder, and error. Use a compatible release rather than renaming an unrelated archive.

lessons.keywords: modules local module plugin extension npm zip archive marketplace hooks

lessons.title: Project and global configuration
lessons.summary: Inspect exactly which instructions and tools a workspace will use.
lessons.location: Settings → Coding → Configuration.
before: Select a workspace, even when inspecting the effective combination with global settings.

steps.title: Choose Project or Global
steps.body: Open the corresponding tab. Use Create/Edit to work on the supported harness.json or harness.jsonc document and its supplied template.

steps.title: Add only the fields you need
steps.body: Configuration supports instructions, references, skills, named agents, memory options, MCP servers, permissions, and plugins within its schema. Keep a small valid change rather than pasting unrelated app settings.

steps.title: Manage bindings safely
steps.body: Use the page’s folder grants, variables, and secret controls for references that need them. Do not put a real secret directly into a file you will commit or share.

steps.title: Validate, inspect, and trust
steps.body: Save a valid document, reload, and inspect Effective configuration, sources, and warnings. Review the resolved project tools and approve only the configuration you intend to run.

lessons.outcome: The effective configuration lists the sources and contributions that apply to the current workspace.
limits: Malformed or unknown fields are rejected. Project and global values combine according to the supported loader rules; inspect the effective result.
A changed tool configuration can need a new trust decision. Loading a file alone does not execute its hooks or connect its servers.

fixes.solution: Read the precise validation error, fix that field, and reload. Remove a stale binding/reference or use the page’s valid starting template.

lessons.title: CodeGraph and the repository map
lessons.summary: Help the assistant navigate a codebase with the right kind of index.
lessons.location: Settings → Coding → CodeGraph; Coding chat settings → repository map.
before: Choose a supported Code workspace with the required command environment.

steps.title: Open Code intelligence
steps.body: Review the current workspace’s index state and available install/index/refresh controls. Prepare the optional tool if the page requires it.

steps.title: Index the project deliberately
steps.body: Run the page’s supported indexing action and wait for completion. Rebuild/refresh when the reported index is missing or stale.

steps.title: Ask a structural question
steps.body: Use Code to ask where behavior lives, who calls a symbol, or which files a change affects. The available graph tools can supplement direct file reading.

steps.title: Review the repository-map preference
steps.body: The compact repository map is a separate context aid under Coding chat behavior. Enable it when you want a symbol overview supplied in prompts.

lessons.outcome: The assistant can use the available project structure tools and/or compact map when relevant.
limits: Language coverage and call resolution are best effort. An index is not a compiler, test suite, or proof of current runtime behavior.
Index generation can consume storage/time and depends on the workspace and environment.

fixes.problem: The graph is missing or stale
fixes.solution: Check the selected workspace, index status, command environment, and the page’s refresh/index result. Direct file exploration is still useful.

lessons.title: Use Caveman’s shorter reply styles
lessons.summary: Install the optional skill pack and choose how terse replies should be.
lessons.location: Settings → Coding → Caveman.
before: Use this when shorter responses suit the task; keep precision for instructions and errors.

steps.title: Install the pack
steps.body: Choose Install Caveman. It uses the app’s existing model connection and does not require another API key, terminal, or proxy.

steps.title: Choose intensity
steps.body: Pick the offered reply intensity. Off removes the style instructions while the separately enabled skills can remain available. Classical Chinese/Wenyan is an optional style variant.

steps.title: Review the coding skills
steps.body: Enable or disable the focused commit, review, investigation, patch, and verification skills individually. They also appear in the skill picker when available.

steps.title: Check results rather than promised savings
steps.body: Use the optional token report if helpful. Increase clarity or switch the style off whenever short phrasing makes an answer difficult to follow.

lessons.outcome: New requests use the chosen reply style and the relevant enabled skills.
limits: Shorter replies do not guarantee lower total cost; style instructions also consume input tokens.
This is an instruction pack, not a new model or a reliable way to eliminate the model’s reasoning tokens.

fixes.solution: Lower the intensity or set it Off. Keep only the coding skills you still want enabled.

lessons.title: Connect your GitHub account
lessons.summary: Sign in or use a personal access token with the right permissions.
lessons.location: Settings → GitHub.
before: A GitHub account with access to the repositories you want to use.

steps.title: Start browser sign-in
steps.body: Choose Sign in with GitHub. When a device code appears, use Copy & open, sign in on GitHub, enter the code, and approve the intended access.

steps.title: Request workflow access only if needed
steps.body: The workflow option is relevant when pushing workflow-file changes. Read the permissions being requested before completing authorization.

steps.title: Use a token if sign-in is unavailable
steps.body: Choose Use personal access token. Create it on GitHub, select the intended repositories, and grant the repository/content permissions needed for your actions. Paste it in the token form and Verify/connect.

steps.title: Confirm the connected account
steps.body: The panel should show the expected GitHub login. Use its disconnect/change-account controls when you want another account.

lessons.outcome: Settings shows the intended connected GitHub account.
limits: Some builds do not have browser sign-in configured; the page offers the token route.
Organization approval, repository roles, token expiry, and branch protections still apply. A token must have the permissions needed by each operation.

fixes.solution: Check repository selection, token scopes/permissions, organization authorization, and expiry. Reconnect only after correcting the access problem.

lessons.title: Import a GitHub repository
lessons.summary: Bring a repository into a new app workspace.
lessons.location: Settings → GitHub → Import from GitHub, or Add workspace → Import from GitHub.
before: A working network connection.
For private repositories, a connected account with repository access.

steps.title: Choose a repository
steps.body: When signed in, pick from the repository list and load more if necessary. Or use Import by URL and paste a GitHub HTTPS URL or owner/repository.

steps.title: Review the import
steps.body: Confirm the repository identity and the destination information in the dialog. Import creates a workspace; it does not overwrite an arbitrary folder you were editing.

steps.title: Wait for preparation and cloning
steps.body: The app can prepare Git tools if they are missing. Keep the app/network available and read progress or errors before retrying.

steps.title: Open the workspace
steps.body: Use Open workspace after success. Check its files, then start a Code task or open project checks.

lessons.outcome: The imported repository is available as a workspace in Projects.
limits: Importing code does not install every dependency or prove the project will build on Android.
Public imports can work by URL without sign-in. Private access still depends on your account and the repository’s rules.

fixes.solution: Check the URL/account, network, storage, and Git-tool preparation message. An empty list does not prove a manually specified accessible repository is invalid.

lessons.title: Review, commit, and push changes
lessons.summary: Publish selected local changes to the intended repository branch.
lessons.location: Code → GitHub control, or Settings → GitHub → Commit & push.
before: Use the repository-root workspace with a GitHub HTTPS origin.
Have push permission and a connected account.

steps.title: Check the repository and branch
steps.body: Open Commit & push and read the repository/branch summary. For an unconnected local folder, connect an existing GitHub repository using the setup controls first.

steps.title: Choose the files
steps.body: Review the change tree, browse folders, and select only the paths you intend to publish. Read the actual diffs in Code/Files before including them.

steps.title: Write a useful commit message
steps.body: Describe the change clearly. Use Commit & push to create the selected commit and send it to the shown remote branch.

steps.title: Check the result
steps.body: Refresh the repository state and read the success/failure. If a commit already exists, Push existing commits retries publication without inventing another change.

lessons.outcome: The selected changes are committed and, when the push succeeds, appear on the intended GitHub branch.
limits: A local commit can succeed while its push fails. Inspect the current state before retrying.
This flow does not force-push or bypass branch protection. It connects an existing repository; it is not a blanket promise to create a new GitHub repository.

fixes.solution: Check permissions, protected branches, and remote changes. Read the error and resolve the branch state instead of forcing an overwrite.

lessons.title: Open a pull request
lessons.summary: Turn a published feature branch into something reviewable.
lessons.location: Commit & push → Create pull request.
before: A connected GitHub repository and account with the required access.
A head branch with commits intended for a different base branch.

steps.title: Review the branch flow
steps.body: Open Create pull request and check the head/source and base/target branches. Confirm which direction the change will merge.

steps.title: Prepare the publication
steps.body: Review any unpushed commits or working-tree requirements shown by the dialog. Push the intended branch when required before opening the PR.

steps.title: Write the request
steps.body: Review/edit the proposed title and body, and choose Draft when you want to signal that the work is not ready for full review.

steps.title: Create and inspect
steps.body: Submit, then use Open on GitHub or Copy link to inspect the actual PR. Check its diff, checks, reviewers, and permissions on GitHub.

lessons.outcome: A successful result shows the actual pull request number/link, or identifies an existing request.
limits: Creating a pull request does not merge it or make tests pass. Review and merge follow GitHub’s own repository rules.
A generated description needs review, especially any claim that a test or verification was performed.

fixes.solution: Check that the branches differ, commits are pushed, the base exists, and your account can open PRs in the target repository.

lessons.title: Save a reusable GitHub push preset
lessons.summary: Repeat a known publication task manually or on a schedule.
lessons.location: Commit & push → Save reusable push preset; navigation menu → Automation.
before: A reviewed repository, branch, and file selection.
Only schedule publication if you intend future changes to be sent without reviewing each occurrence.

steps.title: Capture the intended repository
steps.body: Open the preset action after checking repository and branch. Give it a recognizable name and useful commit message.

steps.title: Choose the path policy
steps.body: Keep selected paths, or explicitly choose Include all future changes when that is truly what you want. Review this choice carefully.

steps.title: Choose its schedule
steps.body: Use Manual, Hourly, or Daily as offered and set the daily time when needed. Save the preset.

steps.title: Manage it in Automation
steps.body: Run it manually first, inspect history, and pause/edit/delete it if the publication scope or schedule changes.

lessons.outcome: Automation has a reusable push task with the repository, branch, and path policy you reviewed.
limits: Including future changes can publish files you have not reviewed at the time the schedule runs.
Android can delay schedules. GitHub authentication, branch state, and protections can block a run.

fixes.solution: Open its history and linked run, then inspect repository state and credentials. Correct the cause before retrying.

lessons.title: Grant only the storage access you need
lessons.summary: Understand private folders, selected folders, and broad file access.
lessons.location: Settings → Coding → Terminal & device → Shared storage; Add workspace for folder grants.
before: Know whether the project lives in app-private storage, shared device storage, or a selected system-picker folder.

steps.title: Start with a private or selected folder
steps.body: An app workspace needs no broad storage grant. System picker can grant a particular folder for file tools without exposing all shared files.

steps.title: Grant broad access when necessary
steps.body: For direct access to shared folders, use the Shared storage action and Android’s All files access screen when offered. Return to the app and refresh/check the state.

steps.title: Recheck the workspace
steps.body: Open Files and confirm that the intended folder can be read and written. Shell commands may need a real filesystem path in addition to a picker grant.

steps.title: Manage permissions separately
steps.body: Review remembered tool grants under Workspace access. Revoke Android storage access in Android settings when you no longer want it.

lessons.outcome: The app has the storage access required by the chosen workspace and reports that access clearly.
limits: All files access does not make another app’s protected private data or every system path readable.
A folder-picker grant, an agent approval, root, and device-owner access are distinct permissions.

fixes.problem: Permission was granted but a folder still fails
fixes.solution: Reopen the folder picker if its grant expired, check SD-card availability, and verify that the path is not protected by Android.

lessons.title: Prepare Linux and install packages
lessons.summary: Add a command environment when your task actually needs one.
lessons.location: Settings → Coding → Terminal & device → Linux environment / package manager.
before: Enough storage and a working connection for environment/package downloads.

steps.title: Install or prepare the environment
steps.body: Open the Linux section and use its setup action. Wait through download, installation, and preparation until the page reports ready.

steps.title: Add the tools for this project
steps.body: Use the package manager controls or an approved package-install task for the runtimes you need, such as Git, Python, Node, or build tools.

steps.title: Check the actual environment
steps.body: Open Terminal in the chosen local workspace and run a small version/check command. The app environment is separate from another terminal app’s private files.

steps.title: Repair only the reported problem
steps.body: If setup fails, read its message, check space/network, and use the offered retry/repair action. Keep important workspace files backed up before removing environment data.

lessons.outcome: The environment is ready and the required commands can run in a compatible workspace.
limits: Linux is optional for ordinary hosted Chat. Installing it does not grant Android root or turn the phone into an unrestricted desktop.
Package availability, CPU architecture, shared-storage behavior, and Android limits affect what can run.

fixes.problem: Install succeeds but a command still fails
fixes.solution: Check that it was installed in the same environment used by the task, that its architecture is supported, and that the workspace has a direct shell path.

lessons.title: Shizuku, Shevery, and normal shell access
lessons.summary: Connect optional shell privileges without confusing them with root.
lessons.location: Settings → Coding → Terminal & device → Shizuku / supported shell provider.
before: A separately installed and running compatible shell provider if you want that route.

steps.title: Start the provider
steps.body: Follow the provider app’s own setup so its service is running. AndroidHarness does not activate it just by being installed.

steps.title: Grant AndroidHarness access
steps.body: Open the shell-provider section and request permission. Approve the intended request in the provider, then refresh the connection state.

steps.title: Wait for a usable connection
steps.body: Permission granted and service ready are separate states. Review connection/startup details if the service reports binding or compatibility problems.

steps.title: Choose the execution route
steps.body: Use the app’s access-mode controls for commands. Check diagnostics when you need to know which route actually ran the last command.

lessons.outcome: The app reports a callable shell connection when the provider is ready and authorized.
limits: Shell-provider access is not automatically root and does not make every protected path accessible.
Provider versions, Android versions, process lifetime, and device firmware can affect connection behavior.

fixes.problem: Permission is granted but commands fail
fixes.solution: Check the service-ready/binding state and connection details. Restart or repair the provider connection using its actual error, then test a harmless command.

lessons.title: Pair wireless debugging
lessons.summary: Connect Android’s wireless ADB route from the app.
lessons.location: Android Developer options → Wireless debugging; AndroidHarness → Terminal & device → Wireless ADB.
before: A supported Android version with wireless debugging available.
A network/device state that allows Android wireless debugging.
Allow pairing notifications for the notification-code flow, or use Manual pairing in connection options.

steps.title: Start pairing from AndroidHarness
steps.body: In Wireless ADB, tap the pairing button. Allow the local-network permission if Android requests it. The app starts looking for Android’s pairing service.

steps.title: Open Android’s pairing-code screen
steps.body: Open Developer options → Wireless debugging, turn it on, and choose Pair device with pairing code. Keep this screen open so the pairing service remains available.

steps.title: Enter the code through the notification
steps.body: Pull down the notification shade, open AndroidHarness’s pairing notification, use its Enter code action, and submit the six-digit code currently shown by Android. Wait for the pairing/connection result.

steps.title: Use manual pairing if needed
steps.body: If notifications are disabled or discovery fails, open Connection options → Manual pairing. Enter the current pairing port and code from Android. A pairing port and a connection port are different values.

steps.title: Verify the connected state
steps.body: Wait for Connected and use the available connection test. If paired but disconnected, use Reconnect. Disconnect or Forget the pairing from connection options when you no longer want it.

lessons.outcome: The app reports an active wireless ADB connection that can serve supported shell/device actions.
limits: Pairing does not root the phone. OEM policies, Wi-Fi changes, debugging state, and Android restarts can interrupt access.
An old pairing port/code is not a permanent connection address.

fixes.solution: Check that wireless debugging is still enabled, use the current connection port, and refresh discovery/reconnect. Generate a new pairing code only when pairing is actually needed.

lessons.title: Use root only where you intend
lessons.summary: Keep root connection, project permission, and task mode separate.
lessons.location: Settings → Coding → Terminal & device → Advanced → Root access.
before: A device that already has a working root manager. AndroidHarness does not root it.

steps.title: Connect through the root manager
steps.body: Use Grant/check access and approve the actual root-manager request. Review the detected manager and connection state.

steps.title: Keep temporary limits when appropriate
steps.body: Temporary root mode can limit access to an app session, chat, or action and allowed projects. Review Project root permissions before letting an agent request it.

steps.title: Choose the route and fallback
steps.body: Review Access mode and Auto fallback. The displayed preference/order applies before a command starts. Check diagnostics for the last route actually used.

steps.title: Stop or disconnect when finished
steps.body: Use the privileged-access controls as appropriate. Treat the root browser as direct access to important device files and inspect paths carefully.

lessons.outcome: Root is available only under the connection and scope choices you explicitly made.
limits: Full access agent mode does not override project root permission or create a root connection.
Turning temporary mode off broadens root availability while connected. Root actions can affect the device beyond a project folder.

fixes.problem: Root unexpectedly falls back or fails
fixes.solution: Check the manager grant, active connection, selected access mode, project permission, and diagnostics before repeating the command.

lessons.title: Understand Dhizuku Device Owner access
lessons.summary: Use its own capability route rather than expecting an ADB shell.
lessons.location: Settings → Coding → Terminal & device → Advanced → Dhizuku.
before: Dhizuku installed and separately activated as Device Owner, if you intend to use it.
Device-owner provisioning is an Android/device-management decision outside this app.

steps.title: Check Dhizuku first
steps.body: Open its own app and verify that Device Owner activation is complete. AndroidHarness’s card reports whether the service is installed, active, or waiting for permission.

steps.title: Grant the connection
steps.body: Use the Dhizuku access request and respond in the provider. Refresh status until the actual result is shown.

steps.title: Use the matching capability
steps.body: Ask Code for a supported device-owner operation and review the tool route/result. Device-owner commands use the dedicated route rather than pretending to be an ordinary privileged ADB shell.

lessons.outcome: The app reports Device Owner access only when the Dhizuku connection is active and granted.
limits: Dhizuku is not root and is not a Shizuku/ADB-shell fallback. Its command execution remains under the provider’s app identity and Android restrictions.
Do not activate device ownership just to try a normal Chat or coding task; it is an optional advanced integration.

fixes.problem: It is connected but a shell command lacks permission
fixes.solution: Check whether the command needs ADB shell or root instead of device-owner app access. Use a supported route for the actual operation.

lessons.title: Build Android projects and inspect device logs
lessons.summary: Prepare the toolchain and use the correct device access.
lessons.location: Code → Android build task; Terminal & device for environment and shell connections.
before: A compatible Android project and the required SDK/JDK/build tools.
A working allowed device route for device-only actions such as protected logs or installation.

steps.title: Prepare the project toolchain
steps.body: Ask Code to inspect the project and install the supported Android build packages/SDK components it actually needs. Read package/toolchain progress and failures.

steps.title: Run the build/check
steps.body: Use the project’s build command in Code or Project checks. Inspect the real command output and generated APK path when successful.

steps.title: Install or launch with the available route
steps.body: Use the app’s supported install/launch action or ask Code to do it. Follow Android’s installer permission/confirmation when the chosen route requires it.

steps.title: Inspect a failure with evidence
steps.body: Use available logcat/device tools for the relevant package and time. Provide the error and reproduce steps, then rebuild and retest any fix.

lessons.outcome: A supported build has a real output file and device checks report actual results.
limits: Android SDK support is tailored to available tools on Android; not every desktop Gradle/NDK project is supported.
A successful APK build is different from a successful install, launch, and functional test. Some device logs/actions need shell or root access.

fixes.problem: A tool or SDK component is missing
fixes.solution: Use the reported missing component and project requirements to prepare it. Avoid repeatedly running the build without resolving the toolchain error.

lessons.title: Schedule a message
lessons.summary: Send a task once or repeat it with a chosen connection and workspace.
lessons.location: Conversation → schedule-message action, or navigation menu → Automation.
before: A saved workspace and working model connection.
Background operation and network access appropriate to the schedule.

steps.title: Write the message
steps.body: Open Schedule message and describe the work to send. Choose the target chat, or a new chat with its workspace.

steps.title: Choose model and timing
steps.body: Review the provider/model and choose the offered repeat option. For a one-time message, pick a future date/time; for a daily schedule, check the time shown.

steps.title: Set the connection requirement
steps.body: Choose any internet or unmetered only. A task waiting for an allowed connection has not necessarily failed.

steps.title: Save and monitor
steps.body: Save the schedule. Open its row or Automation to edit, pause/resume, cancel, or inspect the next/last run and linked conversation.

lessons.outcome: The schedule shows the message, target, timing, and connection policy you chose.
limits: Android scheduling is not exact-to-the-second. Battery restrictions, offline state, force-stop, and device restart can affect when work runs.
A scheduled task still uses model credits and normal tool/access rules. A blocked approval may need you to return to the app.

fixes.solution: Inspect its actual state: waiting for network, queued, paused, blocked, running, or failed. Check background/battery settings and the linked history before creating a duplicate.

lessons.title: Create and monitor an automation
lessons.summary: Pair a clear task with a check and a reviewable run history.
lessons.location: Navigation menu → Automation, or Project → Automation.
before: A workspace, a usable provider/model, and the commands the task needs.

steps.title: Create the task
steps.body: Use the available create/helper or advanced task editor. Give the task a clear name, prompt, target workspace, and intended model.

steps.title: Add an objective check when useful
steps.body: For build/fix workflows, set the actual check command and maximum attempts in the editor. A vague prompt is harder to validate than a command with a useful exit result.

steps.title: Run manually first
steps.body: Test the automation before scheduling it. Inspect its linked conversation, command output, and real result. Adjust the task if it needs clarification or access.

steps.title: Manage ongoing work
steps.body: Use run, pause/resume, edit, cancel, or delete controls as offered. Open History to distinguish passed, failed, blocked, cancelled, and still-running occurrences.

lessons.outcome: The task has a visible configuration and a history entry linked to its actual run.
limits: Automation is limited by Android background scheduling and the same model/tool permissions as interactive work.
A check only proves what it tests. Repeated attempts can use credits and change files; use a suitable project and review the result.

fixes.solution: Read the linked run for its approval, missing dependency, or access problem. Resolve that cause before resuming instead of duplicating the task.

lessons.title: Control a project from Telegram
lessons.summary: Pair your own account and use the same saved chats remotely.
lessons.location: Settings → Telegram.
before: A bot you control, created through Telegram’s official BotFather.
Keep your phone online with AndroidHarness’s Telegram service enabled.

steps.title: Connect the bot
steps.body: Use Create bot if you need the official BotFather link. Paste the bot token into Connect bot and Verify. Keep that token private.

steps.title: Pair your account
steps.body: Start pairing in AndroidHarness, open the bot with the provided link/code, and review the Telegram user identity back in the app before approving it.

steps.title: Choose the work context
steps.body: Set project, chat, provider/model, and Plan/Act in the Telegram settings page or supported bot controls. Send a test message before remote project work.

steps.title: Use the bot controls
steps.body: Send ordinary task messages, use /help for the current commands, and respond to approval/question buttons. /status shows progress; /stop stops work; /retry or /resume handles saved interrupted work where offered.

lessons.outcome: Your paired Telegram account can send work to the chosen app project/chat and receive progress/results.
limits: The bot and your phone need network access. Telegram does not host the AndroidHarness task on your behalf.
Pairing, app tool permissions, model billing, and background settings still apply. Do not run another competing consumer of the same bot token.

fixes.problem: A reply is missing or a request is interrupted
fixes.solution: Inspect Saved work in Telegram settings. Distinguish Retry task from Resend reply, and check Telegram before resending to avoid confusion.

lessons.title: Keep work running and manage notifications
lessons.summary: Choose background behavior and understand Android’s limits.
lessons.location: Settings → Background & notifications; Terminal & device → background/battery controls.
before: Know whether you want tasks to continue when you leave the app.

steps.title: Choose background behavior
steps.body: Open Run in background and set whether agents may continue after you leave. Turning it off stops agents when you leave the app.

steps.title: Choose notification behavior
steps.body: Review the app notification switch and Android notification settings. Grant Android’s notification permission if you want the supported alerts.

steps.title: Review keep-alive and battery policy
steps.body: For long work, inspect Keep alive and the battery-exemption control. Some manufacturers have additional battery/autostart settings you must adjust in Android.

steps.title: Check a real run
steps.body: Start a small task, leave the app, and inspect its actual completion or interruption when you return. Review subagent completion alerts and Live Updates separately where supported.

lessons.outcome: Your settings express whether work should continue, and the app shows the available alerts/progress states.
limits: Android can still stop processes, delay scheduled work, or require a service notice. No switch guarantees permanent background execution.
Live Update presentation depends on Android version, notification permissions, and device support.

fixes.problem: Work stops after the screen turns off
fixes.solution: Check background permission, keep-alive, Android battery restrictions, and the interrupted task’s recovery controls.

lessons.title: Make the app feel like yours
lessons.summary: Choose the layout, theme, palette, and background you enjoy using.
lessons.location: Settings → Appearance.
before: Some wallpaper-color features require a supported Android version.

steps.title: Choose a layout and theme
steps.body: Use the workspace-layout control for the phone/desktop preference. Choose System, Light, Dark, or AMOLED for the theme; wide layouts can show project tools beside the conversation.

steps.title: Choose your colors
steps.body: Use wallpaper-derived colors where supported, a built-in palette, or a custom palette. In custom palettes, save the intended colors, select the palette, and review the preview.

steps.title: Add a Harness Canvas
steps.body: Add a photo/artwork, choose whether it appears in Chat and Code, adjust image dimming for readability, and optionally match app colors to it. Change/remove the image from the same section.

steps.title: Set progress styling
steps.body: Choose flat or squiggly progress bars. Open a conversation and check that text, controls, and progress remain comfortable to read in your chosen setup.

lessons.outcome: The layout and appearance reflect your selected preferences across the supported screens.
limits: Wallpaper colors and hardware/display behavior vary with Android and device support.
Background images and custom palettes can reduce readability if you choose low-contrast content. Use dimming and inspect both conversation and settings surfaces.

fixes.solution: Check whether wallpaper colors, an active custom palette, or Canvas color matching is currently selected.

lessons.title: Tune AH Rumble
lessons.summary: Feel progress without making every event distracting.
lessons.location: Settings → AH Rumble.
before: A device with a vibration motor.

steps.title: Choose where it runs
steps.body: Enable Rumble and choose whether it applies to Chat, Code, or both.

steps.title: Try the feel and strength
steps.body: Use the preview controls to test crisp/smooth feel and strength. The defaults are a useful starting point.

steps.title: Choose engine and events
steps.body: Advanced controls include automatic/built-in/custom haptic engines and per-event patterns/levels for thinking, tools, writing, completion, and requests that need you.

steps.title: Keep bursts comfortable
steps.body: Adjust minimum spacing, writing-flow behavior, battery-saver behavior, and any fine-tuning you need. Reset AH Rumble if you want to return to defaults.

lessons.outcome: The preview and supported conversation events use your chosen haptic behavior.
limits: Motor capability and Android haptic support vary. Unsupported built-in effects can fall back to custom pulses.
The phone’s touch-vibration setting and battery-saver preference can suppress pulses.

fixes.solution: Check the phone has a motor, system touch vibration is enabled, the current Chat/Code scope is selected, and battery saver is not suppressing it.

lessons.title: App lock, screenshots, and secrets
lessons.summary: Choose how the app is protected on this phone.
lessons.location: Settings → Privacy & security.
before: A working Android device lock/authentication method if you want app lock.

steps.title: Enable app lock
steps.body: Turn on the app-lock preference and complete the device authentication requested. Read the unlock behavior before relying on it.

steps.title: Set when it locks again
steps.body: Choose the background auto-lock delay. A short delay is useful when you frequently leave the phone unattended.

steps.title: Choose screenshot behavior
steps.body: Review the screenshots/recents-preview preference. Credential forms can raise their own secure-screen protection even when general screenshots are allowed.

steps.title: Manage credentials at their source
steps.body: Use connection settings to replace or remove keys. Revoke a lost/compromised key at the provider, and review which remote service receives a conversation.

lessons.outcome: The app follows the selected lock and general capture preferences, subject to the secure surfaces it uses.
limits: App lock controls opening the app. It does not encrypt or recall messages already sent to a provider.
A remote model, MCP service, web tool, Telegram, or proxy can receive the data required by its request. Local inference alone does not make all enabled tools offline.

fixes.problem: A screenshot is blocked on a key form
fixes.solution: That form intentionally protects credentials. Close it before capturing the general app screen.

lessons.title: Change the app language
lessons.summary: Use translated controls while keeping model language a separate choice.
lessons.location: Settings → App language.
before: The in-app picker shows the languages bundled with this build.

steps.title: Open the language picker
steps.body: Choose the language you want, or System default to follow Android. Allow the app to refresh its visible labels.

steps.title: Check the selected screens
steps.body: Return to the page you were using. Settings search can match translated labels and English technical keywords.

steps.title: Ask for your preferred reply language
steps.body: Tell the assistant which language to use, or set a Chat instruction. Changing app labels does not force every model response into that language.

steps.title: Contribute if you want
steps.body: Use the language page’s translation/contribution link when offered. Report a specific unclear or missing label with its screen context.

lessons.outcome: The app controls use the selected bundled language wherever translations are available.
limits: These tutorials are currently written in English; untranslated new content falls back to the default language.
Model output, website content, external sign-in pages, and provider errors have their own language behavior.

fixes.problem: I cannot find the old English setting name
fixes.solution: Use Settings search with either the translated label or a distinctive English keyword such as “API”, “memory”, or “notifications”.

lessons.title: Choose what opens when you return
lessons.summary: Set Chat and Code startup behavior independently.
lessons.location: Settings → Chat settings and Settings → Coding.
before: Decide whether you prefer a new conversation or returning to your recent work.

steps.title: Choose the starting section
steps.body: In Chat settings, set the start screen to Chat, Code, or the last selected section as offered.

steps.title: Choose Chat startup
steps.body: Set whether entering Chat starts fresh or resumes the last Chat according to the available choice.

steps.title: Choose Code startup
steps.body: Open Coding and choose its new/resume behavior. Review the current project when returning to a previous Code conversation.

steps.title: Try the next launch
steps.body: Leave and reopen the app to check that the selected behavior fits your workflow. Existing chats remain available in the navigation lists.

lessons.outcome: The app opens the section and conversation behavior you selected when the preference applies.
limits: These choices do not delete old conversations or create a backup.
A missing/removed conversation or workspace can require a fresh choice instead of restoring the old one.

fixes.solution: Review both the section default and that section’s startup choice, then confirm which recent chat/project is still available.

lessons.title: Back up settings and connections
lessons.summary: Export a protected configuration, then review before restoring it.
lessons.location: Settings → Backups → Settings backup.
before: Choose a password you can keep separately from the exported file.
Stop active work before a restore when requested.

steps.title: Choose Export
steps.body: Open Settings backup and export. Enter/confirm the encryption password. Choose whether to include credentials and MCP servers; treat that option as sensitive.

steps.title: Save the encrypted file
steps.body: Choose a destination in Android’s file picker. Keep the password separately; it is needed to unlock the backup.

steps.title: Unlock and review before restoring
steps.body: On Import, choose the file and enter the password. Review the providers, servers, memories, and any sensitive settings before confirming.

steps.title: Check restored connections
steps.body: Read the restore result, review imported endpoints, reconnect excluded account sessions manually, and test only the connections you want to use.

lessons.outcome: You have an encrypted settings file or a reviewed restore result with the imported settings/connections.
limits: GitHub tokens and OAuth sessions are excluded. Local model binaries, project files, and a complete Linux environment are not carried by this backup.
Only restore a trusted file: imported provider endpoints can receive future messages. A partial failure needs inspection before retrying.

fixes.solution: Check the password and original file. Do not repeatedly import a partly restored configuration without reading the reported result.

lessons.title: Export and restore conversation history
lessons.summary: Keep a portable copy of chats and their supported saved context.
lessons.location: Settings → Backups → Chat backup.
before: Pick a safe storage location for a file that contains conversation data.

steps.title: Export the chats file
steps.body: Use Export in Chats backup and choose a destination. Wait for the report showing the exported conversations/messages.

steps.title: Import the original file
steps.body: Choose Import, select the saved backup, and wait for validation. Read any file-format or size error before retrying.

steps.title: Map missing workspaces
steps.body: If the restore asks, map conversations to existing/new workspaces using the restore dialog. Check the destination instead of accepting a similarly named folder blindly.

steps.title: Review the result
steps.body: Read the imported/already-present counts and open a restored conversation. Verify its workspace and current provider before resuming tasks.

lessons.outcome: Supported conversation history is exported or restored, with duplicate handling and workspace mapping reported.
limits: Chat export contains private conversation data. Keep it somewhere appropriate and protect it separately if needed.
It does not include provider API keys or copy all project files, model weights, or remote server data.

fixes.problem: A restored chat cannot continue working
fixes.solution: Connect its provider and map/reopen its workspace. The history file does not recreate the original external environment.

lessons.title: Transfer a folder with FTP or SFTP
lessons.summary: Preview an upload or download before replacing files.
lessons.location: Settings → FTP / SFTP sync.
before: A local workspace with a direct shell/filesystem path.
A remote FTP/SFTP server account and folder you can access.

steps.title: Add the connection
steps.body: Choose the workspace and Add connection. Enter protocol, host, port, username, remote folder, and the supported password/key authentication.

steps.title: Verify the server
steps.body: Use the test/fingerprint controls. For SFTP, check the host fingerprint before trusting it. Save the intended connection.

steps.title: Preview the direction
steps.body: Choose Preview upload to send local files or Preview download to fetch remote files. Read new/replacement/unchanged counts and paths.

steps.title: Apply reviewed changes
steps.body: Enable replacement only if you intend to overwrite the listed existing files, then apply. Read progress/results or cancel when needed; review partial work after an interruption.

lessons.outcome: The previewed files are transferred in the direction you chose and the app reports the result.
limits: FTP sends data/credentials without transport encryption. Use it only on an appropriate trusted network; use SFTP when its secure connection meets your needs.
This is an explicit preview-and-apply transfer, not a promise of continuous two-way synchronization or conflict-free merging.

fixes.problem: Transfer is disabled or the test fails
fixes.solution: Check direct local-path support, server reachability, folder permissions, credentials, and SFTP fingerprint. Review the actual failure before changing direction.

lessons.title: Share a workspace through the FTP server
lessons.summary: Open a temporary file share on the phone you control.
lessons.location: Settings → FTP server.
before: A local workspace with a direct filesystem path.
A trusted network if you choose to allow LAN connections.

steps.title: Choose the share
steps.body: Select the workspace, a valid port, username, and password. Keep Read only enabled unless uploads/changes are intended.

steps.title: Choose who can reach it
steps.body: Leave local-only behavior for same-device access, or explicitly enable LAN access when another device on your network should connect.

steps.title: Start and connect
steps.body: Tap Start, then use the displayed address, username, and active-share password in your FTP client. Check the shown workspace and client count.

steps.title: Stop when finished
steps.body: Use Stop share after the transfer. Recheck files if you allowed writes; keep the phone and required service available while sharing.

lessons.outcome: The app shows a running share with its address and connection information until you stop it.
limits: This is FTP, not SFTP/HTTPS; it does not encrypt credentials or file contents in transit.
Sharing is scoped to the selected local workspace. It does not make a picker-only/remote workspace a hosted public file service.

fixes.solution: Check LAN is enabled, both devices can reach each other, the displayed address/port is current, and the network does not isolate clients.

lessons.title: Free space with a reviewed cleanup
lessons.summary: Remove regenerable files without guessing which folders are safe.
lessons.location: Settings → Storage.
before: Pause relevant work before deleting caches or build outputs.
Use Local models to remove individual model weights.

steps.title: Measure first
steps.body: Open Storage and tap Rescan. Each category lists its items with sizes and paths, and Largest shows the biggest ones. Open Not measured to see anything the scan could not read and why.

steps.title: Inspect the candidates
steps.body: Open Review cleanup and inspect each proposed path/category. Select only caches, build output, or verified unused managed-package content you intend to remove.

steps.title: Check package requirements
steps.body: Open a Linux package under Linux packages and tap Requirements to see its recorded requirements and dependencies before releasing a requirement or removing eligible unused files.

steps.title: Confirm the exact cleanup
steps.body: Read the confirmation and run it. The app checks paths again and skips changed/unavailable/linked items it cannot safely remove. Rescan to see the result.

lessons.outcome: The result reports removed files/space and any items that were skipped.
limits: Regenerated caches may download again and builds may take longer after cleanup.
Source folders, models, history, recovery data, and required/unknown package ownership are protected by this cleanup policy; it is not a full device cleaner.

fixes.solution: There may be no eligible regenerable data, or ownership/requirements cannot be verified. Do not manually delete protected folders to imitate the cleanup.

lessons.title: Understand tokens, costs, and cache figures
lessons.summary: Use the stats as evidence with clear accounting limits.
lessons.location: Settings → Usage; conversation → Context & limits or /cost where supported.
before: Some values depend on usage/pricing metadata supplied by the provider.

steps.title: Open the statistics
steps.body: Review the displayed token, provider/model, time, and cost summaries. Use available date/group/filter controls to focus on the work you care about.

steps.title: Inspect a specific conversation
steps.body: Use its context/usage details or supported cost command for the current task. Include subagent/retry work when assessing an expensive task.

steps.title: Read cached-token numbers carefully
steps.body: Cached input counts describe provider accounting when reported. They are different from deleting local app/download caches.

steps.title: Confirm charges at the provider
steps.body: Use the provider’s official usage/billing dashboard for actual bills, credit balances, and account-side spending controls.

lessons.outcome: You can connect the app’s reported usage with the tasks and models that produced it.
limits: Missing prices, incomplete usage metadata, currency, discounts, and provider billing rules can make app cost estimates incomplete.
A low output-token count alone does not describe all input, thinking, tool, retry, or subagent costs.

fixes.problem: A price or token count is missing
fixes.solution: Check whether the provider reports it and whether the app has pricing metadata. Use the provider dashboard for billing evidence.

lessons.title: Start with the troubleshooting page
lessons.summary: Check the failing layer before changing unrelated settings.
lessons.location: Settings → Troubleshooting.
before: Note what you tried, which screen failed, and the exact visible error.

steps.title: Check the required connection first
steps.body: Review the selected provider/model and workspace. Use Check models or Check folder when relevant; a connected account does not prove every model or write operation works.

steps.title: Review optional components separately
steps.body: Linux, shell providers, SSH, MCP, notifications, and Live Updates have their own states. Optional features can remain off when your task does not use them.

steps.title: Open the matching repair/settings page
steps.body: Use the page’s action for the component that needs attention. Retry the smallest failing operation after correcting its reported cause.

steps.title: Collect a useful report
steps.body: Copy/share the troubleshooting report if you need support. The report excludes credentials, addresses, file paths, and chats; add a clear description and redacted reproduction steps yourself.

lessons.outcome: You know which component failed and have either a successful focused retry or a useful diagnostic report.
limits: A ready status is narrower than a full functional test: folder checks may be read-only, tool discovery is not tool execution, and installed Linux is not a tested command.
The /doctor agent shortcut performs a different, broader tool test and can create temporary fixtures in its workspace.

fixes.problem: Everything looks ready but the task still fails
fixes.solution: Capture the exact failing tool/command/request and its output. Check the workflow’s actual prerequisites instead of treating readiness as proof.

lessons.title: Read the provider request log
lessons.summary: See the exact call that failed and what the provider answered.
lessons.location: Settings → Provider request log.
before: Capture is off by default. Reproduce the problem once with it on, or the page stays empty.

steps.title: Turn capture on
steps.body: Switch capture on at the top of the page, then send the failing message from any chat and come back. Only traffic recorded while capture is on shows up, so enable it before the attempt you want to see.

steps.title: Read the request before the reply
steps.body: Each entry lists the endpoint, method, status and timing, which separates a 401, 429 or 400 from a slow or truncated stream. Filter by chat or by text when the list gets long.

steps.title: Include bodies only for the request you are chasing
steps.body: Prompts, replies and raw stream events are large and private. Turn Include bodies on for one attempt, read it, then turn it off again. Without it the log keeps only URLs, headers and status.

steps.title: Keep it or take it with you
steps.body: Capture lives in memory and is cleared when the app closes. Export or Save to file writes a readable log you can paste into a bug report; Keep on this device stores it encrypted for the next session.

lessons.outcome: You can point at the failing request, say which side produced the error, and keep a log that shows it.
limits: The log holds HTTP traffic only. Local models never send requests, so their runs never appear here.
Credentials are masked and storage paths become placeholders, but prompts and replies are your own text; read a saved log before sharing it.
Capture adds work to every request. Leave it off when you are not chasing something.

fixes.solution: Confirm capture is on, confirm the chat uses a cloud provider, then send a new message. Requests made before capture was enabled were never recorded.

lessons.keywords: request log trace http capture debug

lessons.title: Fix a failed model connection
lessons.summary: Read the error type before replacing keys or paying for more access.
lessons.location: The failed conversation/tool result; Manage providers → affected connection.
before: Do not include full API keys or authorization headers in a support message.

steps.title: Check identity and access errors
steps.body: For authentication/permission errors such as 401/403, verify the provider, key, enabled-key state, project/organization, expiry, and model permissions.

steps.title: Distinguish rate and billing limits
steps.body: A rate-limit error may need waiting or fewer requests. A billing/credit/usage-cap error needs the provider account’s access or funding corrected. Repeating the request alone will not fix it.

steps.title: Check model and input compatibility
steps.body: For missing-model or invalid-input errors, refresh the catalogue and check the exact ID, protocol, context size, image support, tool support, and thinking options.

steps.title: Check the network separately
steps.body: For timeout, DNS, TLS, or connection errors, inspect the connection, endpoint, proxy, and service availability. Test one short request after the intended correction.

lessons.outcome: The smallest test either succeeds or leaves a specific error you can investigate without exposing secrets.
limits: An HTTP code alone can be ambiguous across providers; read the provider’s error message and official guidance.
Changing to another provider can send context to another service and incur its usage charges.

fixes.problem: I cannot tell which connection failed
fixes.solution: Read the conversation’s model/header and fallback activity, then inspect that exact saved provider rather than an unrelated default.

lessons.title: Updates, setup, and app information
lessons.summary: Find your version, reconnect setup, and understand support options.
lessons.location: Settings → Updates, Setup guide, or About.
before: A network connection for update checks and external support pages.

steps.title: Check the installed version
steps.body: Open About or Updates to see the actual installed version/build. Include that version when describing a reproducible problem.

steps.title: Use the offered update path
steps.body: Check for updates and read the release details. Use the download/install action offered for this distribution and follow any Android installer step.

steps.title: Revisit setup when needed
steps.body: Use Setup to review the onboarding choices and required permissions/connections. Check each choice rather than assuming a reinstall is necessary.

steps.title: Find credits and support
steps.body: About lists source/licence/credits and available support or donation links. A donation supports the app; it does not buy API credits or a provider subscription.

lessons.outcome: You know the installed version, available update/setup path, and where the app’s own information lives.
limits: Update delivery and installation behavior differ by distribution and available device permissions.
An app update cannot guarantee new access to an external model, fix a provider outage, or restore deleted files.

fixes.solution: Check the exact installer/download error, available storage, install permission, and distribution/signature compatibility. Keep existing data backed up before changing installations.

lessons.title: What AndroidHarness can and cannot do
lessons.summary: Separate app capabilities from model promises and device permissions.
lessons.location: Use this checklist before choosing a workflow.
before: The app is a harness: it connects models, context, tools, and the access you grant.

steps.title: Choose a supported kind of work
steps.body: Chat can answer, write, research, discuss attachments, use supported inline visuals, and manage allowed conversational context/settings. Code can inspect/edit accessible projects and use its supported commands and integrations.

steps.title: Check the model and environment
steps.body: The chosen model must support the required tools/images/protocol. Local models need compatible weights and sufficient device resources. Builds and local services need compatible runtimes.

steps.title: Check the real permission boundary
steps.body: Workspace access, Android storage, shell-provider access, root, Device Owner, service accounts, and API billing are separate layers. One permission does not silently grant the others.

steps.title: Verify the outcome
steps.body: Read tool results, inspect changed files, run checks, and test the behavior. Ask the assistant to distinguish what it actually verified from what still needs testing.

lessons.outcome: You can tell whether a task is supported, needs setup, or requires another tool/service.
limits: The app cannot guarantee correct answers, unlimited free APIs, every model format, every desktop build, permanent background execution, or arbitrary control of other apps.
It cannot bypass a provider’s payment/access rules, a website login/paywall, Android’s security model, or repository protections. Models can be wrong about their own success.

fixes.problem: The assistant promises something that is not visible
fixes.solution: Ask for the actual file, tool result, test output, or link. If no supporting result exists, treat the work as unverified and narrow the request.

lessons.title: Read activity, progress, and verification
lessons.summary: Tell a real tool result apart from thinking or a promise.
lessons.location: A running conversation → activity/tool cards; Settings → Coding → Code conversation & commands.
before: Activity describes the current run; inspect its result before assuming work succeeded.

steps.title: Open the activity you need
steps.body: Expand a tool card/group to inspect its request, output, and error state. Thinking blocks and timing/token details describe the model’s response, not an independent verification.

steps.title: Follow the task and package progress
steps.body: Use the displayed task list, package-install progress, browser activity, and subagent cards to see what is actually running or waiting for you. Answer a question/approval when one is blocking progress.

steps.title: Review live code carefully
steps.body: The Show live code preference controls previews of code/edit activity while the run is in progress. A live preview is not a saved final file; inspect the completed diff and file after the tool finishes.

steps.title: Check the verification receipt
steps.body: Expand Verification after Code work. Passed, failed, unconfirmed, and recheck-needed results refer to recorded commands. Read which command was checked and rerun it after further changes.

lessons.outcome: You can identify the active step, inspect an actual failure, and see what was or was not verified.
limits: A finished tool call can still contain an error. A task-list checkmark or fluent final answer is not proof that a build, test, or visible behavior passed.
Large outputs can be shortened in the card; use the available output reader or ask for the relevant portion. Optional run tips are guidance, not completed actions.

fixes.problem: The answer says a check passed but the receipt is unconfirmed
fixes.solution: Ask for the actual command/output or run the check yourself. A check may also need rerunning if files changed after it.

lessons.title: Read and research GitHub in Chat
lessons.summary: Ask about repositories, files, issues, or pull requests without importing a project.
lessons.location: Chat → ask about a GitHub URL or owner/repository; Settings → GitHub for private-account access.
before: Use a connected account for private data and requests that require authentication. Public reading can work without sign-in.

steps.title: Give a precise repository or link
steps.body: Paste the repository, file, issue, pull request, or release link and ask what you want to know. Include the branch or commit when a particular version matters.

steps.title: Ask for evidence from GitHub
steps.body: Chat can use its read-only GitHub search, file, and REST-reading tools to inspect accessible material. Ask it to point to the file or discussion supporting the explanation.

steps.title: Check the referenced version
steps.body: Open the links and compare the branch/commit with what you intended. Search and API access have their own restrictions and rate limits.

steps.title: Move to Code for changes
